units.tr: To the most noble man, Mr. Daniel Studer, patrician of St. Gall, etc., his honoured patron, greetings: Caspar Waser.

units.la: NON arbitror, quenquam esse, qui non acerbissimo dolore saepe apud se reputet luctuosam faciem praesentis tempestatis, & proximè praeteritae: in qua Christi Ecclesia tot discriminibus, periculis, difficultatibus & persecutionibus, toto ferè orbe, affligitur, ut cum sanctissimo Jeremia nemo non optimo jure exclamare possit, O utinam redigat aliquis caput meum in aquam, & oculos meos in scaturiginem lacrymarum[?] tum deflerem interdiu & noctu confessos filiæ populi mei.
units.tr: I do not think anyone exists who does not often reflect with the bitterest grief on the sad face of the present tempest and of the one just past, in which the Church of Christ is afflicted by so many dangers, perils, difficulties and persecutions across nearly the whole world. So with the most holy Jeremiah, anyone may rightly cry out: "O that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people."

units.la: Ista recordatio fecit, ut cogitanti mihi, quid hac recurrente vice, de Scholæ nostræ instituto, disquisitioni publicæ solenni subicerem, animum meum subierit, haud ἀπροσδιονύσως[?] facturum me, si præsentem de Persequutionibus Ecclesiæ Dissertationem in aspectum lucemque proferrem.
units.tr: That thought made me, while I was considering what I should set before the public solemn disputation this coming round, concerning the arrangement of our school, realise that I would not be acting unseasonably if I brought out into the light my present dissertation on the persecutions of the Church. [ἀπροσδιονύσως]

units.la: Tibi verò illam inscribere, nobilissime STUDERE, volui, quòd scirem his re[?] studiis delectari[?], & in sacra ac profana historia, unde illa depromptæ sunt, versatum esse, ac proinde dextrè de eis judicare posse. Studio quinetiam habui, isto, ceu publico symbolo, testari, benevolentiam tuam, quam de propagandâ amicitiâ, quæ aliquammultos annos cum optimo cognato tuo felicis memoriæ, Dn. JACOBO STUDERO, Senatorii ordinis viro, mellinia[?] sanè mihi intercesit, sponte obtulisti, gratam acceptamque exstitisse. Te, obsecro, leve munus, leve si pauculas chartas spectes, sed tamen argumenti dignitate grave, & his temporibus apprimè accommodum, nec non devoti in te animi plenum boni consulas, placideque accipias. Deus te, & honoratissimam familiam tuam sospitet & superstitet diu diu.
units.tr: I wanted to dedicate it to you, most noble Studer, because I knew that you delight in such studies and are well versed in sacred and profane history, from which these matters are drawn, and so are able to judge them rightly. I was also eager to bear witness, by this as a public token, to the goodwill you freely offered me concerning the furthering of a friendship which has existed between us for some years, through your excellent cousin of blessed memory, Mr. Jacob Studer, a man of the senatorial order. I beg you to accept this slight gift, slight if you look at the few pages, yet weighty by the dignity of its subject and most suited to these times, and to take it kindly and receive it favourably, as the full expression of my devoted mind toward you. May God keep you and your most honourable family safe and sound for a long, long time.

units.la: PERSEQVTIONVM nomine cōplectimur quæcunq; à persequutoribus malignè fiunt in injuriam & contumeliā hominum fidelium: quæ multa sunt ac varia: veluti odia, inimicitiæ, falsæ accusationes, convitia, carceres, vincula, exilia, relegationes, confiscationes bonorum, mors denique ipsa, & hujus diversa immania tormenta ac supplicia; quibus corpus illi quidem necare, at animæ damnum nullum inferre possunt.
units.tr: By the name of persecutions we embrace whatever is maliciously done by persecutors to the injury and reproach of faithful people. These are many and various: such as hatreds, enmities, false accusations, insults, prisons, chains, exiles, banishments, confiscation of goods, and finally death itself, together with its various monstrous torments and punishments. These can indeed kill the body, but can inflict no harm on the soul.

units.la: II. Hujusmodi persequutionib. tam vetus Ecclesia in veteri, quàm nova in novo Test. semper exagitata fuit.
units.tr: II. The Church of the Old Testament has always been harassed by persecutions of this kind, just as the New Testament Church has been in the New.

units.la: III. VETERIS Ecclesiæ persequutiones fuere cùm particulares, tùm universales.
units.tr: III. The persecutions of the Old Testament Church were both particular and universal.

units.la: IV. Particulares; quæ in certas personas exercebantur: veluti in Abelem, Isaacum, Iacobum, Iosephum, Davidem, Eliam, Esajam, Ieremiam, Danielem ejusq; socios, aliósve summæ sanctitatis & authoritatis viros: qui persequutores suos capitales habuere Kaïnum, Ismaëlem, Esavum, suos met fratres germanos, Saulem, Izabelem, Nabuchodonosorem, & alios Libycæ arenæ numero carentes.
units.tr: IV. Particular persecutions were those directed against certain persons, such as against Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, David, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and his companions, and other men of the highest holiness and authority. Their chief persecutors were Cain, Ishmael, Esau, their own full brothers, Saul, Jezebel, Nebuchadnezzar, and others more numerous than the sands of Libya.

units.la: V. Universales; quæ exercebantur in Iudæorum gentem universam: quo in numero præcipuè fuere persequutiones à Pharaonibus in Ægypto, à regibus Assyriorum in Babylonia, & Antiochis in Syria instituta atq; agitata: quæ scelleratissima Tyrannorum cohors, nihil petulantiæ, contumeliæ, injuriæ, crudelitatis & immanitatis, quibus Dei Ecclesiam funditus exstirparent, intermisit.
units.tr: V. Universal persecutions were those raised against the whole Jewish nation. Among these, the persecutions set on foot and pursued by the Pharaohs in Egypt, by the kings of the Assyrians in Babylonia, and by the Antiochuses in Syria were chief. This most wicked band of tyrants left no insolence, insult, injury, cruelty or savagery untried, by which they might root out the Church of God from its foundations.

units.la: VI. Hoc quàm verissimum esse, ex omni veteri historia constat, præsertim Pentateuchi, Regum, Prophetarum, Macchabæorum & aliorum: idémque locupletissimè testantur Psaltis[?] valdè pathetica verba, O Deus, ingressæ sunt gentes in hæreditatem tuam: polluerunt templum sanctum tuum: redegerunt Hierosolymam in acervos: dederunt cadavera servorum tuorum in cibos volucribus cœli, carnem beneficorum tuorum bestijs terræ: effuderunt sanguinem eorum velut aquam circa Hierosolymam; nec erat qui sepeliret: facti sumus opprobrium vicinis nostris, sanna & ludificatio iis; qui circa nos sunt, &c. item Apostoli ad Hebræos: Alij verò fustuario[?] multati sunt, non accipientes liberationem, ut meliorem resurrectionem acciperent: alij rursus ludibria & flagella sunt experti, insu- per & vincula & carcerem : alij lapidati, ferrâ dissecti sunt, cremati sunt, gladio cæsi occubuerunt : oberraverunt cum ovillis & caprinis pellibus : destituti,pressi,malè habíti; quí- bus indignus erat Mundus:in desertis errantes,& montibus ac speluncis, & cavernis terræ. Vide Psal. 79, & Hebr. 11,35, 36,37,&c.
units.tr: VI. That this is most true is clear from all ancient history, especially the Pentateuch, the Kings, the Prophets, the Maccabees and others. The Psalms also bear the fullest witness to it, in the very moving words: "O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps. The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them. We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us," etc. Likewise the Apostle to the Hebrews: "Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover, of bonds and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, they were tempted, they were slain with the sword; they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented; of whom the world was not worthy: they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth." See Ps. 79 and Heb. 11:35, 36, 37, etc.

units.la: VII. NOVAE Ecclesiae persequutiones fuere ei partim à Iudæis ipsis intentatæ : partim ab Imperatoribus Romanis : partim à Pontificibus Romanis. De Hæreticis enim, qui & ipsi Ecclesiam vehementer afflixerunt, hîc quæstio non est.
units.tr: VII. The persecutions of the New Church came partly from the Jews themselves, partly from the Roman emperors, and partly from the Roman pontiffs. As for the heretics, who also greatly afflicted the Church, the question is not concerned with them here.

units.la: VIII. In persequutionibus, quas Iudæi Ecclesiæ inflixerunt, numeratur prima Iudæorum regis, HERODIS Magni : qui tum ipsummet DOMINVM ad necem sceleratam quæsivit, tum omnes puellos Bethlehemiticos bimulos inauditâ feritate trucidavit.
units.tr: VIII. Among the persecutions which the Jews inflicted on the Church, the first is that of Herod the Great, king of the Jews, who both sought the Lord himself for a wicked death and slaughtered with unheard-of savagery all the male children of Bethlehem under two years old.

units.la: IX. Altera refertur HERODIS Antipæ, Magni filii, Iudæorum tetrarchæ; qui sævi parentis sæva vestigia [?] pressit. Quum enim sanctissimus vir, Iohannes Baptista, quo Sol non vidit magis pium, incestos ejus nexus jure taxâsset, optimum ille tanti viri caput à cervice revellit, quum putida meretrix vincla necemq; ei parâsset. quo scelere non exsaturatus atrox parricida, unâ cum Pilato, Clero, & Senatu Populoq; Iudaico, Mundi servatorem jam adultum, indignissimo ausu persequi non cessavit: donec improba coluvies in medium cæli terræque levatum ignominiosæ cruci tandem affixerunt & necârunt.
units.tr: IX. The second is that of Herod Antipas, son of the Great, tetrarch of the Jews, who trod in the savage footsteps of his savage father. When the most holy man John the Baptist, than whom the sun has never seen a more pious man, had rightly rebuked his incestuous union, he had that excellent head of so great a man cut from his neck, since the foul harlot had prepared chains and death for him. Not satisfied with this crime, the fierce parricide, together with Pilate, the clergy, the Senate and the Jewish people, did not cease with most unworthy audacity to persecute the Saviour of the world, now grown to manhood, until that wicked brood at last fixed him, raised up between heaven and earth, to the shameful cross and killed him.

units.la: X. Tertia censetur Concilii HIEROSOLYMITANI: quod non tantùm sanctos Apostolos vinculis multavit, & flagris cruentavit, sed etiam lapidum grandine sanctum Stephanum interemit: propterea quòd multis gravibus rationibus, maximè exemplo Abrahæ, piorum patrum & Dei ipsius testimonioq; Mosis, solidè atq; evidenter probavit, Deum templo & ritibus Mosis per se non delestari, necutrunq; perpetuò durare velle.
units.tr: X. The third is counted as that of the Council of Jerusalem, which not only put the holy Apostles in chains and bloodied them with scourges, but also killed holy Stephen with a hail of stones, because it had solidly and clearly proved, by many weighty arguments, chiefly the example of Abraham, the testimony of the pious fathers and of God himself and of Moses, that God does not in himself delight in the temple and the rites of Moses, nor wish either to endure forever.

units.la: XI. Quarta numeratur HERODIS Agrippæ, Magni nepotis; qui ut gratum faceret Iudæis, Petrum Apostolum in carcerem conjecit: capite verò truncavit Iacobum Majorem, filium Zebedæi, fratrem Iohannis Evangelistæ, primum inter Apostolos martyrii lauream adeptum; quem paucis annis post, anno nempe LXIII. glo-riosè infequutus est Iacobus Minor, Episcopus Hierosolymitanus, frater DOMINI, cognomento justus, filius Mariae, sororis Virginis Mariae: quì e templi fastigio præcipitatus, atque inter lapidandum fullonis fuste percussus atq; occisus perhibetur.
units.tr: XI. The fourth is that of Herod Agrippa, grandson of the Great, who, to gain the favour of the Jews, cast the Apostle Peter into prison, and beheaded James the Greater, son of Zebedee, brother of John the Evangelist, the first among the Apostles to win the crown of martyrdom. A few years later, in the year 63 to be precise, James the Less followed him gloriously: bishop of Jerusalem, brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, son of Mary, sister of the Virgin Mary. He is said to have been thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple, and, while being stoned, struck and killed with a fuller's club.

units.la: XII. Iudaeorum perfequutiones mox subsequutae sunt IMPE-RATORVM & CAESARVM Romanorum: quae perplures fuere. Quum enim Satan, [?]ἀγριόθυμῳ ille & [?]δαιμονὸς & veritatis hostis, hanc funditus exstirpare omni ope niteretur, excitavit Neronem, Domitianum, Trajanum, Antoninum Verum, Severum, Maximinum, Decium, Valerianum, Aurelianum, Diocletianum et Maximianum, ingentia Naturae monstra; quibus ad persequendos Christianos, ceu strenuis carnificibus, est usus. Quantas enim illi caedes, occisiones, strages, lanienas, quàm indignas, magnas, horribiles ediderint, qui dicere vellet, hunc tempus citius quàm oratio deficeret.
units.tr: XII. Soon after the persecutions of the Jews came those of the Roman EMPERORS and CAESARS, which were very many. For when Satan, that fierce-minded and demonic enemy of the truth, strove with every means to root it out from its foundations, he stirred up Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Antoninus Verus, Severus, Maximinus, Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, Diocletian and Maximian, monstrous creatures of Nature, whom he used as vigorous executioners to persecute the Christians. For the slaughters, killings, massacres, butcheries, so unworthy, great and horrible, which they carried out, would take more time to describe than a speech would last.

units.la: XIII. Prima Imperatoria persequutio sub NERONE exstitit, impurissimo illo hominis propudio: qui Christianos tanto furore infestatus est, ut non modò funestum Romae incendium, quod sex diebus & totidem noctibus continenter arsit, cujus author & autoptes ipsemet esse voluit, ita Trojae incendium videre se gestiens, insontibus imputaret: sed publico etiam in eos edicto, Romae & in omnibus provinciis, stirpitus exscindendos, velut hostes Deorum, et urbis incendiarios mandaret. quod initium duntaxat laniena fuit. Nam paulò post aliquos ludibrii causa tergoribus ferarum insui, & canibus ad lacerandum objici præcepit: alios exuri: alios suspendi & crucifigi: nonnullos aliis suppliciis mactari voluit, ut, quemadmodum Tacitus scribit, ipsamet Romana plebs ingenti erga illos misericordia afficeretur. Primipilares martyres, hac grassante tempestate, fuere Petrus Apostolus; qui cruci dicitur affixus pedib. in cælum erectis: & Paulus Apostolus, illud [?]σκεῦος τῆς ἐκλογῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ; qui capite plexus est Romae anno LXX. et universa Ecclesia Christiana, Hierosolymae id temporis congregata; quae anno ante, nempe LXIX. divinitus monita, in oppidum Pellam, trans Iordanem situm, patriae dulci solo pulsa, dissipataque fuit.
units.tr: XIII. The first imperial persecution took place under NERO, that most impure disgrace of a man, who was so assailed by fury against the Christians that he not only blamed the innocent for the deadly fire at Rome, which burned for six days and as many nights without stop, whose author and spectator he himself wished to be, eager to see the burning of Troy in the same way, but also by a public edict commanded that they be utterly exterminated in Rome and in all the provinces as enemies of the gods and incendiaries of the city. This was only the beginning of the butchery. For soon after, for the sake of mockery, he ordered some to be sewn into the hides of wild beasts and thrown to dogs to be torn apart, others to be burned, others hanged and crucified, and some he wished to be put to death by other punishments, so that, as Tacitus writes, the Roman populace itself might be moved by immense pity for them. The chief martyrs in this raging storm were the Apostle Peter, who is said to have been crucified with his feet raised toward heaven, and the Apostle Paul, that [chosen vessel of God, σκεῦος τῆς ἐκλογῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ], who was beheaded at Rome in the year 70; and the whole Christian Church, gathered at Jerusalem at that time, which, warned by God the year before, that is in the year 69, was driven from its dear native soil into the town of Pella, situated beyond the Jordan, and scattered.

units.la: XIV. Altera sub DOMITIANO obtinuit. Quum enim ille blasphemo ore Deum se jactare non erubesceret, & sic appellari ac coli vellet ab omnibus, pedes quin etiam, quod nemo Caesarum ante ipsum, praeter unum Domitianum[?] post ipsum, petierat, osculari sibi jussisset: Christianos, qui solum Deum adorabant, nullis non tormentorum exquisitissimorum generibus, excruciavit ac sustulit. Obtinentes hac carnificina Iohannes Apostolus, quum ferventis olei aheno percoctus incolumis evasisset, in Pathmum est relegatus, ubi Apocalypsin vidit: Timotheus Ephesi lapidibus interemtus: Dionysius Areopagita Parisiis, Gervasius & Protasius Mediolani gladio necati fuerunt.
units.tr: XIV. The second persecution came under DOMITIAN. When he was not ashamed to boast with a blasphemous mouth that he was God, and wanted to be called and worshipped as such by all, he even ordered that his feet be kissed, which no Caesar before him had demanded, except one Domitian after him; he tortured and destroyed the Christians, who worshipped God alone, with every kind of most exquisite torment. In this slaughter the Apostle John, after being boiled in a bronze vessel of boiling oil, escaped unharmed, and was banished to Patmos, where he saw the Apocalypse. Timothy was stoned to death at Ephesus; Dionysius the Areopagite was killed at Paris; Gervasius and Protasius were beheaded at Milan.

units.la: XVI. Tertia coepit sub TRAJANO: qui Christianos stirpi-tus eradicandos censuit, propterea quod templa, aras, sacrificia, imagines, dies festos, totamque religionem Romanam improbarent & detestarentur: e contrario Deum unum adorarent, Christum Dei fili-um sospitatorem unum colerent; idque in spiritu & veritate: unde immenso illi numero ad varias miseras mortes rapti trucidatique sunt. Inter hos Simeon Hierosolymitanus Episcopus, annos natus centum viginti in crucem acti, Ignatius Episcopus Antiochenus Romae in Circo bestiis dilaniandus objecti, Quirinus militum tribunus, Sulpitius, Eustachius, Sophia cum tribus filiabus Fide, Spe et Charitate, Sabina item, victoriosam mortem Redemtoris sui causa oppetiverunt.
units.tr: XVI. The third began under TRAJAN, who decided that the Christians should be utterly uprooted, because they rejected and abhorred temples, altars, sacrifices, images, festival days, and the whole Roman religion; on the contrary, they worshipped one God and honoured Christ the Son of God, the one Saviour, and did so in spirit and in truth. Therefore that vast number were carried off to various wretched deaths and butchered. Among these were Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem, who was crucified at the age of one hundred and twenty; Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, who was thrown to the beasts in the Circus at Rome to be torn apart; Quirinus, a military tribune; Sulpitius, Eustachius, Sophia with her three daughters Faith, Hope and Charity; and likewise Sabina, all of whom met a victorious death for the sake of their Redeemer.

units.la: XVI. Memorabile cumprimis est, quod de Ignatij martyrio hi-storia ecclesiastica memorat, hoc loco minime praetereundum. Ille, ubi cum bestiis sibi confligendum vidit, alacri plane & laetabundo animo, et martyrii desideratissimo, Optarem, inquit, iam iam bestiis illis frui, quae ad me dilaniandum paratae sunt. Mihi est in votis eas brevi reperire, quas valde blande compellabo, ut me carptim & absque mora devorent, neque à me dentes abstine-ant, ut à quibusdam; quos metu perculsae non auderent attingere. Quòd si illae recusent me adoriri, ego ipse eas instigabo. Date vos mihi veniam. Quid mihi profuturum, equidem non ignoro. Iam incipio Christi discipulus esse: facessat à me rerum omnium sive oculis subiectarum, sive eorum aciem fugientium admiratio, ut Iesum Christum assequar. Ignis, crux, bestiarum conflictationes, ossium distractiones, concisiones membrorum, totius corporis tanquam molitae farinae attritiones, omnia deniq; suppliciorum genera, à Diabolo excogiexcogitata, in me coacervantur, ut Iesum Christum duntaxat adipiscar, &c.
units.tr: XVI. Church history records something memorable about the martyrdom of Ignatius, which must not be passed over here. When he saw that he had to fight with the beasts, with a truly eager and joyful spirit, and with the most longed-for desire for martyrdom, he said: "I wish that I might now at once enjoy those beasts that are prepared to tear me apart. I pray that they will quickly find me, and I will coax them very gently to devour me at once, and not hold back their teeth from me, as they have from some whom they were too afraid to touch. But if they refuse to attack me, I myself will urge them on. Forgive me; I know well what will be of use to me. Now I am beginning to be a disciple of Christ. Let the admiration of all things, whether placed before our eyes or fleeing from their sight, depart from me, so that I may attain Jesus Christ. Fire, the cross, the assaults of beasts, the tearing apart of my bones, the cutting of my limbs, the grinding of my whole body as if it were milled flour, in short, all the kinds of punishment devised by the Devil, be heaped upon me, provided only that I obtain Jesus Christ," etc.

units.la: XVII. Quarta persecutio sequuta est, in Imperium succedente ANTONINO VERO, Philosopho. quo tempore hostes Christianorum, ingenti molimine connixi, fulminis instar in eos irruere, atq; dirissime grassando rem gessere, nullus non omnino strenuus, nullus non adversus in Christianos. unde acriter saevitum: sed quod saevum certamen indigne abstulit imperterritos alioqui Christi athletas Polycarpum Smyrnensis Ecclesiæ pastorem, Asiæ doctorem & Christianorum id temporis patrem communem, Iustinum Philosophum, Irenæum Episcopum Lugdunensem, Maturum, Pothenum, Attalum, Blandinam, & alios: qui cum alibi, tum imprimis Lugduni & Vienna in Gallis[?], ubi omnium gravissime saevit tempestas, atrocibus & diuturnis cruciatibus excruciabantur: propterea quod ne latum unguem a fide orthodoxa discedere vellent, tam magno & constanti animo, ut non dubitarint ipsam etiam Ethnicæ religionis vanitatem palam improbare & taxare.
units.tr: XVII. The fourth persecution followed, when ANTONINUS VERUS, the philosopher, succeeded to the empire. At that time the enemies of the Christians, straining with a huge effort, rushed upon them like a thunderbolt, and acted with the most dreadful fury; there was no one who was not thoroughly vigorous, no one who was not hostile to the Christians. Thus they raged fiercely; and this cruel conflict unworthily carried off Polycarp, minister of the church of Smyrna, teacher of Asia and at that time the common father of the Christians, who were otherwise fearless athletes of Christ; also Justin the philosopher, Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, Maturus, Pothinus, Attalus, Blandina, and others. They were tortured with savage and lasting agonies, both in many other places and especially at Lyons and Vienne in Gaul, where the storm raged most severely of all. The reason was that they would not depart a hair's breadth from the orthodox faith, and with such great and steadfast spirit that they did not hesitate openly to condemn and censure the very vanity of the heathen religion.

units.la: XVIII. Memorabile hic est, quod de nonagenarii prope senis Polycarpi martyrio eadem historia narrat. Quum enim proconsul Romanus bestiarum laniatus illi minitaretur, Accerse illas, inquit, pius martyr: nam nobis rata ac decreta stat sententia: & multum ab eo absumus, ut aliquando animo mutato, nos meliorum poeniteat quo deteriora sequamur. Quū proconsul instaret At vero te ardentibus flammarum incendiis domitū & mansuetum reddā, si bestiarū laniatus contemnas, & non resipiscas ocyus[?]: ille invicto animo Ignem mihi minitaris, qui ad tempus exardescit quidem, sed paulo post penitus exstinguitur: verum ignem illum futuri iudicii, ad perpetuum impiorum supplicium ac cruciatum reservatum, omnino ignoras. Sed quid cunctaris? Profer bestias, aut aliud quod lubet, &c. Hîc quum rogo exstructo, manibus a tergo circumplicatis constrictusq; firmè teneretur, & clavis etiam esset affigendus, Sinite me, inquit, hoc modo: nam qui mihi patientiam ad ignis flammas sustinen-das pro sua clementia largitur largietur etiā, ut sine cōmissu-ris clavorum, quibus me affigere statuitis, constans absque ulla corporis commotione rogo adhærescam. Tibi vero, pater dilecti filii tui Iesu Christi, per quem tui cognitionem accepimus, gratias ago, quòd me huius diei & horæ celebritate donasti, in qua cum in martyrum numero, tum in calice passionis Christi tui, tormentorum particeps fiam, in resurrectionem vitæ æternæ, tam animæ, quam corporis, per immortalem Spiritus sancti virtutem, &c.
units.tr: XVIII. Here is something memorable that the same history relates about the martyrdom of Polycarp, an old man of nearly ninety years. When the Roman proconsul threatened him with being torn by beasts, he said: "Bring them on, pious martyr, for our sentence stands fixed and decided, and we are far from changing our minds and repenting, to pursue worse things instead of better." When the proconsul pressed him: "But I will tame you and make you gentle with the burning flames of fire, if you despise the mauling of beasts and do not repent quickly," he answered with an unconquered spirit: "You threaten me with fire, which blazes for a time but is quickly extinguished altogether; but you are wholly ignorant of that fire of the coming judgment, reserved for the eternal punishment and torment of the wicked. But why do you delay? Bring forth the beasts, or whatever else you please," etc. When he was bound, with his hands tied behind his back, firmly held on the pyre that had been built, and was about to be fastened with nails too, he said: "Leave me as I am; for he who grants me the patience to endure the flames of the fire will also grant, by his mercy, that I may stand firm on the pyre without being fixed by the nails you intend to fasten me with, and without any movement of the body. And to you, Father of your beloved Son Jesus Christ, through whom we have received the knowledge of you, I give thanks, that you have granted me to share in this day and hour, in which I shall be a partaker of the tortures, both among the number of the martyrs and in the cup of the passion of your Christ, unto the resurrection of eternal life, both of soul and of body, through the immortal power of the Holy Spirit," etc.

units.la: XIX. Quanta in adeundo ac subeundo martyrio Blandinæ magnanimitas et constantia fuerit: itidem ex historia ecclesiastica liquet. Hæc enim ad omnia cruciamentorum genera quasi lætitia gestiens, ac de ipso vitæ suæ exitu permagno gaudio exsultans properabat: non quasi ad bestias crudeliter projecta, sed ad cœnam sponsi amicè invitata. Post verbera, post bestiarum laniatus, post sartaginis exustionem, ad extremum in rete involuta, tauri ictib. objectatur. Quæ quum ab animali illo diu multumque icta exagitataq. fuisset, ac nullum sensum haberet tormentorum, quæ hactenus ei obtigissent, partim propter spem, quam Dei promissis firmè adhærescebat, partim propter colloquia, quæ intra se cum Christo conferebat, tandem ensejugula-ta fuit. unde gentes ipsæ palàm testabantur, mulierem apud se nun-quam tot tamque acerba tormenta tam viriliter & constanter tolle-râsse ac superâsse.
units.tr: XIX. How great was the magnanimity and constancy of Blandina in undertaking and enduring martyrdom is likewise clear from church history. For she, rejoicing as if exulting in all kinds of torments, hastened towards the very end of her life with great joy; she went not as one cruelly thrown to the beasts, but as one kindly invited to the bridegroom's feast. After the scourgings, after the mauling by beasts, after being burned on the gridiron, at last she was wrapped in a net and offered to a bull's blows. When she had been struck and tossed about by that animal for a long time, and felt no sense of the torments that had befallen her until then, partly because of the hope to which she firmly clung in God's promises, and partly because of the conversations she held within herself with Christ, at last she was slain with the sword at the throat. Thus the very nations openly testified that a woman had never among them endured and overcome so many and so bitter torments so manfully and steadfastly.

units.la: XX. Stridente hac procellâ, quæ Dei ὑπεραρρήτῳ[?] & est miseri-cordia, exorti sunt, tanquam amœnissimæ Plejades, aliquot doctissimi viri, qui apologeticis suis Christianorum innocentiam, fidemque ac religionem masculè asserebant, propugnabant, celebrabant. Tales fuere Quadratus, Aristides, prædictus Iustinus, Asianus, Apollinaris, Athenagoras, Apollonius, Tertullianus, & alii, qui divinis suis libellis, quos Imperatoribus, Senatui et Præsidibus Rom. obtulerant, hoc tandem obtinuere, ut litteras ab Impp. ad Asiæ præsides exaratas, ne quam Christianis porrò molestiam aspergerent, vetarent, nisi qui convicti essent, tentâsse quidpiam contra Rempubl. Rom.
units.tr: XX. While this storm was raging, which is by God's unspeakable [ὑπεραρρήτῳ] mercy, there arose, like most lovely Pleiades, several very learned men who, in their apologies, boldly asserted, defended and celebrated the innocence, faith and religion of the Christians. Such were Quadratus, Aristides, the aforementioned Justin the Asian, Apollinaris, Athenagoras, Apollonius, Tertullian, and others, who by their divine little books, which they had offered to the emperors, the Senate and the Roman governors, finally obtained this: that the emperors issued letters to the governors of Asia forbidding them from further harassing the Christians with any trouble, unless they were convicted of having attempted anything against the Roman commonwealth.

units.la: XXI. Verumenimvero ἀντιζήλῳ[?] & ille, ὡς βάσκανος[?] & ἀντινει-μάχῳ[?] & τῷ γένει τῶν δικαίων, neque dum exsaturatus fuit. Nam ad Imperii gubernacula sedente SEVERO quinta persequutio excitata atq; severè exercitata fuit. quæ præter alios illustres fidei Christianæ assertores Leonidem patrem Origenis, Heraclidem & Heronem excarnificavit. Chartagine, famosâ illâ Africæ urbe, Perpetua & Felicitas bestiis objecta, atque ab illis dilaniatae sunt.
units.tr: XXI. But that one too, being jealous [ἀντιζήλῳ] like an envious man [βάσκανος] and an adversary [ἀντινεμάχῳ] of the race of the just, was not yet satisfied. For under SEVERUS, who sat at the helm of the empire, a fifth persecution was stirred up and severely carried out. Besides other illustrious champions of the Christian faith, it butchered Leonides, the father of Origen, Heraclides and Heron. At Carthage, that famous city of Africa, Perpetua and Felicitas were thrown to the beasts and torn to pieces by them.

units.la: XXII. Sexta ab Imp. MAXIMINO suscepta fuit praecipue in Doctores & Episcopos Christianorum. Facillimum enim fore ratus est Tyrannus, ut ipsa tota fides Christiana mox evanesceret, si antistites ejus e medio tollerentur: ut etiam custodibus ovilus remotis, in oves unctosq; Christi tanto liberius involare, eosq perdere pos-set. quod tamen nefarium institutum, Dei benignitate, non successit.
units.tr: XXII. The sixth was undertaken by the emperor MAXIMINUS, especially against the teachers and bishops of the Christians. For the tyrant thought it would be very easy for the whole Christian faith to vanish at once if its leaders were removed from the midst; and that, with the shepherds of the flock removed, he could more freely rush in upon the sheep and anointed of Christ and destroy them. However, this wicked plan did not succeed, by God's goodness.

units.la: XXIII. Septima fuit commota ab Imp. DECIO. Hic promulgatis in toto Imp. sanguinolentissimis edictis, magno numero viros praeclaros ad supplicia raptavit: cujus truculentissimo aevo aliquis nihil audiverit, nisi truncare, mutilare, laniare, deturbare, urere, assare, confodere, concidere, occidere, & quae sunt hujus generis alia ab ipso Orco excogitata tormenta infinita. Inter alios Sixtus Episcopus Romanus capite truncatus, ejus diaconus Laurentius in craticula assatus, Hippolytus a feris equis dilaceratus, Serapion multis prius vulnerib. concisus, tum ex adium suarum summitate praeceps datus fuit. Macarius, Alexander, Epimachus vivi exusti: multae ornatissimae virgines miserabiliter prius excruciatae, postea occisae sunt, veluti Apollonia, Eugenia, Victoria, Theodora, Anatolia, Ruffina, & aliae complures.
units.tr: XXIII. The seventh was stirred up by the emperor DECIUS. He, having published most bloody edicts throughout the empire, dragged great numbers of distinguished men to punishments. In his most savage age, one would have heard of nothing but cutting off, maiming, mangling, casting down, burning, roasting, stabbing, hacking to pieces, killing, and other endless torments of this kind devised by Orcus itself. Among others, Sixtus, bishop of Rome, was beheaded; his deacon Laurence was roasted on a gridiron; Hippolytus was torn apart by wild horses; Serapion, cut with many wounds beforehand, was then thrown headlong from the top of his houses. Macarius, Alexander and Epimachus were burned alive; many most distinguished virgins, first wretchedly tortured, were afterwards killed, such as Apollonia, Eugenia, Victoria, Theodora, Anatolia, Ruffina, and many others.

units.la: XXIV. De Babyla Antiocheno Episcopo, viro aetate gravi, [?]ἀξιομνημονεύτως refert Chrysostomus, quod quum ipse et filii ejus idolis sacrificare recusassent, capitis damnati fuerint. Pater ad supplicium ductus, ut filii prius necaretur voluit, ne forte paterni supplicii magnitudine territi juvenes a fide resilirent. Hic ergo miser pater miserandae necis dulcissimorum filiorum spectator una cum uxore fuit; & quidem magna voce filios est consolatus, adque constantiam hortatus: tum & ipse truncatus, postquam Psalmi verba, Revertere anima mea in requiem tuam, recitasset.
units.tr: XXIV. Chrysostom relates, worthy of remembrance, concerning Babylas, bishop of Antioch, a man advanced in years, that when he and his sons refused to sacrifice to idols, they were condemned to death. The father was led to execution, but he wished that the sons be put to death first, lest the young men, frightened by the severity of their father's punishment, should fall away from the faith. This wretched father, then, was a witness of the pitiable death of his most beloved sons, together with his wife. He indeed comforted the sons with a loud voice and exhorted them to constancy. Then he himself was beheaded, after he had recited the words of the Psalm, "Return, O my soul, unto your rest."

units.la: XXV. Octava persecutio concitata fuit sub Imp. VALERIANO. qui etsi primis Imperii annis mitis erga Christianos exstitit: tamen postea a mago quodam Aegyptio persuasus, non illos solum acerbe est persecutus, sed etiam magicis artib. deditus, ab isto nebulone tenella infantium viscera dissecare, humanasq; hostias mactare didicit. Dominante ista fluctuatione submersi sunt Cornelius Romae in Italia Episcopus, & Cyprianus Carthaginensis in Africa, duo splendidissima Ecclesiae luminaria, quo tempore inauditum antea & horri-ficum excoriationis supplicium contra fideles usurpari coepit, si forte hoc modo à fide Christianâ ad Ethnicam abduci possent. Id vero nequissimi persecutores inusitatis illis immanitatibus obtinere quum non valerent, insidiosis voluptatum illecebris innocentiam Christia-norum foedare, sicque ad lapsum eos impellere sunt nixi, formosas illis mulieres offerentes, quae ad improbam libidinem eos inflamma-rent. Refert Hieronymus, quemdam hujus temporis martyrem lingu-am sibi dentibus abscidisse, eamq; in faciem ejusmodi mulieris exspu-isse, ut ab ea liberaretur.
units.tr: XXV. The eighth persecution was stirred up under the emperor Valerian. Although in the first years of his reign he was mild towards the Christians, afterwards, being persuaded by a certain Egyptian magician, he not only persecuted them bitterly but, given over to magic arts, learned from that scoundrel to dissect the tender entrails of infants and to slaughter human victims. During this tempest Cornelius, bishop of Rome in Italy, and Cyprian of Carthage in Africa, two most splendid lights of the Church, were drowned. At that time a new and hitherto unheard-of and horrible punishment of flaying began to be used against the faithful, if perhaps in this way they might be drawn away from the Christian faith to the heathen one. But when these most wicked persecutors could not achieve this by those unprecedented savageries, they strove to defile the innocence of the Christians by insidious enticements of pleasure, and so to drive them into a fall, offering them beautiful women who would inflame them to shameless lust. Jerome relates that a certain martyr of this time bit off his own tongue with his teeth and spat it into the face of such a woman, so that he might be delivered from her.

units.la: XXVI. Nona ab Imp. AVRELIANO indicta, sed morte ejus interrupta fuit: unde inter decem persequutiones à quibusdam non numeratur.
units.tr: XXVI. The ninth persecution was declared by the emperor Aurelian, but it was interrupted by his death; for this reason some do not count it among the ten persecutions.

units.la: XXVII.Decima sub Impp. DIOCLETIANO & MAXI-MIANO excitata praecedentibus & diuturnior fuit & crudelior. Nam anno Imperii Diocletiani decimo nono, mense Martio, instante festo dominicae passionis, oratoria Christianorum solo aequari, sacra Biblia cremari, & qui publicis fungebantur honoribus deponi, privati vero libertate orbari publico edicto jubebantur. Non multo post alio edicto mandatum, ut Ecclesiarum pastores in vincula tra-derentur, & omnibus adhibitis machinis ad sacrificandum idolis adi-gerentur. Magnis igitur agminibus omnes Christiani cum summi, tum infimi, ad idolorum templa, eorumque sacrificia raptati, & qui cultui illic vacare recusabant, verberibus & gladiis caesi sunt. Tandem edicta de tollendis Christianis ita exasperabantur, ut uno mense martyrum millia septendecim, exceptis exulibus, miserandum in modum trucidata sint. Unus Riciomarus[?], Diocletiani dux, tantam vim sanguinis Christianorum profudit, ut Mosella, undosus Germaniae fluvius, ad sex milliaria martyrum cruore tinctus rubue-rit, & putei complures cadaveribus eorum Coloniae Agrippinae re-pleti fuerint. Tyri in Palaestina, Thebaide in Aegypto, Nicomediae in Bithynia, in Syria, Arabia, Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Ponto, & alibi ubique gentium & locorum, omnes carceres, omnia loca pub-lica civitatum plena erant Christianis captivis, qui vel belluis obje-cti[?], vel duabus inflexis arboribus utrinque pedibus alligati, ut iis de-inde in altum redeuntibus dilacerarentur, fuerunt. Portentosa alia tormenta ac supplicia, quæ Eusebius nono & decimo capitib. octavi libri commemorat, brevitatis causa omitto.
units.tr: XXVII. The tenth persecution, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, was both longer and more cruel than those before it. For in the nineteenth year of the reign of Diocletian, in the month of March, near the feast of the Lord's Passion, by public edict it was ordered that the oratories of the Christians be levelled with the ground, the holy Bibles burned, and those who held public offices be deposed, while those in private life be deprived of liberty. Not long after, another edict commanded that the ministers of the churches be handed over to chains and, with every machine brought to bear, be driven to sacrifice to idols. Therefore, in great throngs, all Christians, both high and low, were dragged to the temples of the idols and to their sacrifices, and those who refused to attend to the worship there were beaten and put to the sword. At last the edicts for removing the Christians were so intensified that in a single month seventeen thousand martyrs, not counting the exiles, were slaughtered in a pitiable manner. One Riciomarus, a general of Diocletian, shed such a flood of Christian blood that the Moselle, a river of Germany abounding in waves, reddened, tinged with the blood of martyrs for six miles, and several wells at Cologne Agrippina were filled with their corpses. At Tyre in Palestine, at Thebais in Egypt, at Nicomedia in Bithynia, in Syria, Arabia, Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Pontus, and elsewhere in every land and place, all the prisons and all the public places of the cities were full of Christian captives, who were either thrown to the wild beasts or, with their feet tied to two trees bent down on either side, were torn apart when the trees sprang back up on high. Other portentous torments and punishments, which Eusebius recalls in the ninth and tenth chapters of the eighth book, I omit for the sake of brevity.

units.la: XXVIII. In Phrygia quadam urbe, Christiani omnis ordinis, sexus & ætatis, Imperatoris exercitu cincti, succensi & vivi combusti sunt, ut ne unus evaserit. Alexandriæ Dorothea virgo nobilis atque modestia inclyta, & aliæ virgines morum castimonia clara, quæ libidini persequutorum non acquiescebant, excruciata & cæsæ fuerunt. Romæ nobilis matrona Sophronia, conjux præfecti urbi, manu suâ mori maluit, quàm ab impuro Tyranno violari. Quid istâ spuman-te lanienâ acciderit Sylvano Tyrio, Petro Alexandrino, Luciano Antiocheno atque aliis viris clarissimis & de Ecclesiâ optimè me-ritis, nemini non notum.
units.tr: XXVIII. In a certain city of Phrygia, Christians of every rank, sex, and age were surrounded by the emperor's army, set on fire, and burned alive, so that not one escaped. At Alexandria the virgin Dorothea, noble and renowned for her modesty, and other virgins famous for the purity of their lives, who would not submit to the lust of the persecutors, were tortured and beaten. At Rome the noble matron Sophronia, wife of the prefect of the city, preferred to die by her own hand rather than be violated by the impure tyrant. What happened amid this foaming butchery to Sylvanus of Tyre, Peter of Alexandria, Lucian of Antioch, and other most illustrious men who deserved very well of the Church, is known to everyone.

units.la: XXIX. Eximia historia de Thebæa legione, à Thebis Ægypti urbe sic dictâ, legitur in veteri quodam Martyrologio, Petro de Natalibus, Vincentio & aliis, digna quæ huic loco inseratur: Evocatus à Maximiano ex Orientis partibus venit dux Mauritius cum eâ legione, ut ingenti exercitu, quem undiquaque conscripserat, Bagandas Imperio rebelles opprimeret Maximianus: qui Christianos propterea rebelles judicabat, quòd fidem Christi abjicere, & idolis immolare recusarent, atque in hos facilius in Occidente, quàm in Oriente sævire se posse existimabat. Erant autem in hac legione viri in rebus bellicis strenui, virtute nobiles, sed fide nobiliores, ut qui Christiana religionis ritum ab Hierosolymitana urbis Episcopo susceperant. Hi exercitum Imperatoris per Alpes in Galliam usque sequuti sunt. Castra autem Cæsar constituit non procul ab Octoduro, quod oppidum in Valesia situm LX. fere millib. passuum à Genevesi urbe distat: ibiq; dæmonibus suis Maximianus sacrum instituit, convocavitque omnes ad id tum Orientis, tum Occidentis milites, seriò mandans per Deorum aras jurarent, pugnare velle se & adversus Bagandas rebelles, & Christianos Diis Imperatoris inimicos persequi. Nuntiatur Imperatoris mandatum Thebanorum quoq; exercitui, qui ad Rhodanum amnem, in loco, quem Agaunum dixere, consederat: sed Octoduro accedere non vult: & secum singuli certò constituunt, animósque obfirmant, eo loci exstingui se, quàm aut Diis sacrificare, aut contra Christianos arma sumere, malle. Quod & animo intrepido Maximiano accersenti eos, sacramenti militaris nomine & religione respondent: hoc insuper addentes, misisse quidem Thebæos ad Imp-eleciam militum legionem, verum cum hoc mandato, ut in bellis justis Imperatorem juvarent, contra Christianos nequaquam arma moverent, sed seipsos potius defenderent contra injustam violentiam. Ibi tum ira percitus Tyrannus decimum quemq; ejus legionis gladio caedi jussit: cui illi certatim ingenti cum laetitia cervices suas objecere. Addidit hoc ipsum factum magnum & animi & fidei robur Mauritio, qui milites confestim gravissima concione ad constantiam & fortitudinem exhortatus est. Qui rursus accersiti Imperatori responderejusserunt, Suscepisse se arma pro Reip. defensione, non contra Christianos: quod ad sacra vero Idolorum attineret, vitam eripi sibi potí-ùs commissuros, quam Deum se pernegaturos, aut daemonum sacrificiis religionem suam contaminaturos. Iubet igitur ad supplicium postulari Tyrannus iterum decimum quemq;, & caeteros nihilominus ad haec, quae spreverant, compelli. Quibus mandatis denuò in castra perlatis, segregatus est atque percussus qui decimus forte obvenerat: reliqua vero se se militum multitudo mutuo sermone instigabat, ut in tam praeclaro opere perfisterent. Maximiano igitur insania adhuc æstuanti hujusmodi mandata mittunt: Milites sumus, Imperator, tui, sed non tam servi, quam liberi, confitemur Deum: tibi militiam debemus, illi innocentiam: à te stipendium laboris accipimus, ab illo exordium sumsimus. Sequi Imperatorem in hoc nequaquam possumus, ut authorem negemus Deum, utique authorem nostrum, Dominum velis nolis & tuum. Sed non in tam funestam rem compellimur, ut in hoc eum offendamus: tibi, ut fecimus hactenus, adhuc parebimus; sin aliter, illi parebimus potius, quam tibi. Offerimus in quemlibet hostem manus, quas sanguine innocentum cruentare nefas dicimus. Dextræ istæ pugnare adversus impios atque inimicos sciunt, laniare pios & cives nesciunt. Meminimus nos pro civibus potius, quam adversus cives arma sumsisse. Pugnavimus semper pro iustitia, pro pietate, pro innocentum salute. Haec fuerunt hactenus nobis pretia periculorum. Pugnavimus pro fide: quam quo pacto conservamus tibi, si hanc Deo nostro non exhibemus? Iuravimus primum in sacramenta divina; iuravimus deinde in sacramenta regia. Nihil
units.tr: XXIX. A remarkable story about the Theban legion, so called from Thebes, a city of Egypt, is read in an old martyrology, in Peter de Natalibus, Vincent, and others, and is worth inserting here: Summoned by Maximian from the regions of the East came the commander Maurice with that legion, so that Maximian might crush with a huge army, which he had enrolled from every quarter, the Bagaudae who had rebelled against the empire. He judged the Christians to be rebels for this reason, that they refused to abjure the faith of Christ and to sacrifice to the idols; and he thought that he could rage against them more easily in the West than in the East. Now in this legion there were men vigorous in warfare, noble in courage, but nobler still in faith, for they had received the rite of the Christian religion from the bishop of Jerusalem. They followed the emperor's army across the Alps as far as Gaul. Caesar pitched camp not far from Octodurum, a town situated in the Valais about sixty miles from the city of Geneva; and there Maximian held a sacrifice to his demons, and summoned all the soldiers, both of the East and of the West, earnestly ordering them to swear by the altars of the gods that they would fight against the rebel Bagaudae and pursue the Christians, enemies of the gods of the emperor. The emperor's command was announced also to the Theban army, which had encamped at the river Rhône, in a place called Agaunum; but they did not wish to come to Octodurum. And each of them firmly resolved with himself, and steeled their spirits, that they would rather be destroyed on that spot than either sacrifice to the gods or take up arms against the Christians. When Maximian summoned them, with fearless spirit they answered him in the name and by the religion of their military oath, adding this besides: that indeed the Thebans had been sent to the emperor's chosen troops, but with this charge, that they should help the emperor in just wars, but should never take up arms against Christians; rather they should defend themselves against unjust violence. Then the tyrant, stirred to anger, ordered every tenth man of that legion to be struck down with the sword; and they, eagerly and with great joy, offered their necks to it. That very deed added great strength of spirit and faith to Maurice, who at once exhorted the soldiers, in a most solemn address, to constancy and fortitude. When they were summoned again and ordered to answer the emperor, they replied that they had taken up arms for the defence of the commonwealth, not against Christians; but as for the sacred rites of the idols, they would sooner surrender their lives than deny God or defile their religion with sacrifices to demons. The tyrant therefore ordered that every tenth man be again demanded for punishment, and that the rest be compelled nonetheless to do the things they had spurned. When these orders were carried back into the camp, the man who by chance had fallen as the tenth was separated out and struck down; but the rest of the multitude of soldiers urged one another, in mutual speech, to persevere in so glorious a work. So to Maximian, still seething in his madness, they sent this message: "We are soldiers, Emperor, yours, but not so much slaves as free men; we confess God. To you we owe military service, to him our innocence; from you we receive the pay for our labour, from him we took our beginning. We cannot follow the emperor in this, to deny God, the author of us both, who is Lord of you as well, whether you will or no. But we are not forced into so deadly a matter as to offend him in this. To you we will still render obedience, as we have done hitherto; but if otherwise, we will obey him rather than you. We lift our hands against any enemy, but we say it is wrong to stain them with the blood of the innocent. These right hands know how to fight against the impious and the enemies, they do not know how to tear the godly and fellow citizens. We remember that we took up arms for our fellow citizens rather than against them. We have always fought for justice, for piety, for the safety of the innocent. These have hitherto been the rewards of our dangers to us. We have fought for the faith: how can we keep it faithful to you, if we do not show it to our God? We first swore by the divine sacraments; then we swore by the royal sacraments. Nothing

units.la: nobis de secundis credas necesse est, si prima perrumpimus. Christianos ad poenam per nos requiri iubes, jam tibi ex hoc alii requirendi non sunt. Habes hic nos confitentes Deum Patrem & Filium eius Iesum Christum, & Spiritu sanctum credimus. Vidimus laborum nostrorum socios, nobis quoque eorum sanguine aspersis, trucidari ferro, & tamen sanctissimorum commilitonum mortes & fratrum funera non flevimus, non doluimus, sed potius laudavimus, & gaudio prosequuti sumus, quia digni habiti essent pati pro Domino Deo eorum. Non nos vero haec ultima necessitas cogit: non nos adversum te, Imperator, armavit ipsa, quae fortissima est in periculis, desperatio. Tenemus ecce arma, & non resistimus tibi, quia mori, quam occidere malumus, & innocentes interire, quam noxii vivere praeponimus, si quid in nos ultra statueris, si quid adhuc iusseris, si quid admoveris, ignes, tormenta, ferrum, subire parati sumus. Christianos nos confitemur: persequi Christianos non possumus. Quum haec Maximianus audivisset, obstinatosque in fide Christi cerneret animos Thebaeorum, desperans gloriosam eorum constantiam posse revocari, omni bellua cruentior, iterum ad ingenii sui saevitiam rediit, atq; una sententia interfici omnes decernit. Immisit igitur in Legione exercitu suum omnem, tam pedestrem, quam equestrem, ac cinctam undiquaq;[?] jugulari praecepit. Caedebantur itaque passim gladiis non reclamantes, sed & depositis armis cervices persequutoribus, & intectum corpus offerentes, non vel ipsa suorum multitudine, non armorum motione elati sunt, ut ferro conarentur afferre injustitiae causam, sed haec solum reminiscentes, se illum confiteri, qui nec reclamando ad occisionem ductus est, & tanquam agnus non aperuit os suum, ipsi quoque tanquam grex dominicarum ovium, laniari se, tanquam ab irruentibus lupis, passi sunt. Neque ulla unquam rabies tantam humanorum corporum stragem dedit.
units.tr: You need not believe us as to what comes second, if we break through what comes first. You order Christians to be called to account for punishment through us; from this, others need not be called to account. Here you have us confessing God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ, and we believe in the Holy Spirit. We have seen the companions of our labours, sprinkled with their blood as we were, cut down by the sword; yet we did not weep for the deaths of these most holy comrades in arms and the funerals of our brothers, we did not grieve, but rather praised them and followed them with joy, because they were judged worthy to suffer for the Lord God. It is not this final necessity that compels us; it is not despair, which is the strongest of all in dangers, that has armed us against you, Emperor. Behold, we hold arms, and we do not resist you, because we prefer to die rather than kill, and to perish innocent rather than to live as guilty men. Whatever you decree against us further, whatever you order, whatever you apply, fire, torments, or the sword, we are ready to endure. We confess that we are Christians; we cannot persecute Christians. When Maximian had heard this, and saw that the minds of the Theban soldiers were obstinate in the faith of Christ, despairing that their glorious constancy could be recalled, he returned to the savagery of his nature, more cruel than any beast, and decreed that all of them be killed with a single sentence. He therefore sent his whole army into the legion, both infantry and cavalry, and ordered them to be slaughtered, surrounded on every side. So they were cut down with swords here and there, not protesting, but even laying down their arms and offering their necks and unprotected bodies to their persecutors. Neither the great number of their own men nor the stirring of arms moved them to take up the sword and so give a cause for injustice. Instead, remembering only that they confessed him who, without protest, was led to slaughter, and like a lamb did not open his mouth, they too, like a flock of the Lord's sheep, suffered themselves to be torn apart as if by attacking wolves. No rage has ever brought about such a slaughter of human bodies.

units.la: XXX. Quid illa ipsa tempestate acciderit Felici & Regulae, fratribus germanis, et Exsuperatio, inconcussae fidei heroibus, neminem, vel mediocriter in annalibus nostratibus versatum, latet. Etsi enim illi è lanienâ modo commemorata evasere, unâ cum Victore et Vrso qui Soloduri postmodum capitis supplicium sunt passi: tamen à Decio, præside Rom. in arce Tigurina habitante, tandem gladio interemti sunt: in quam urbem, superatis Lepontiis alpib. per agrum Glaronen-sem secundo lacu pervenère, circa annum Domini CCXCV. ubi incolis urbis, tum Ethnicis & Idololatris, veram religionem integrum decennium purè fideliterq; prædicârunt, quæ fides sanctorum martyrum inde à mille trecentis viginti septem annis, ab ipsis tradita, et sanguine eorum obsignata, in ecclesia Tig. singulari beneficio, etiam num hodie salva integraq; retinetur ac docetur.
units.tr: XXX. What happened in that very storm to Felix and Regula, brother and sister, and Exsuperantius, heroes of unshaken faith, is hidden from no one who is even moderately versed in our national annals. For although they escaped the butchery just mentioned, together with Victor and Ursus, who afterwards suffered execution by the axe at Solothurn, they were nevertheless at last slain by the sword by Decius, the Roman governor residing in the citadel of Zurich. They reached that city, having crossed the Lepontine Alps and passing through the territory of Glarus and by the second lake, around the year of the Lord 295. There, over a full decade, they preached the true religion purely and faithfully to the city's inhabitants, who were then heathen and idolaters. This faith, handed down by these holy martyrs and sealed with their blood from that time, that is, for 1327 years, is still preserved and taught today, intact and safe, in the Church of Zurich by a singular blessing.

units.la: XXXI. His atq; aliis sævis persequutionib. Ecclesia Dei ab Impp. & Tyrannis Rom. tribus circiter seculis horrendum in modum afflictata fuit, usq; ad tempora Imp. Constantini M. qui decimo Imperii sui anno turbatæ Ecclesiæ halcyonia quadam dedit: donec Imp. Julianus apostata, & Imp. Valens, camerinâ denuo moventes, armis & sophisticationib. suis, novas strages fecerunt. Nam præter plurima crudelitatis ipsorum exempla, quæ plenius in Hist.trip. apud Ruffinum, Theodoretum, Sozomenum & alios videre liceat, illo etiam tum ævo multi insignes Christi servi palmam martyrii consequuti sunt: in quo nobili grege celebrantur Gregorius Alexandrinus, Eusebius, Nectarius, Zenon, Basilius, Ancyranus, Cyrillus Hierolymitanus, etc. Aegypti urbe complures honestæ virgines nudæ in theatrum productæ, deinde dissectæ, & avenâ ac hordeo repletæ porcis ad laniandum objectæ fuerunt.
units.tr: XXXI. By these and other savage persecutions, the Church of God was afflicted in a dreadful manner by the Roman emperors and tyrants for about three centuries, until the time of Constantine the Great, who in the tenth year of his reign gave the disturbed Church a kind of halcyon calm. But then the apostate Emperor Julian and the Emperor Valens, stirring the pot again with their arms and their sophistries, produced fresh slaughters. Besides the many examples of their cruelty, which may be seen more fully in the Tripartite History in Rufinus, Theodoret, Sozomen and others, many distinguished servants of Christ also won the palm of martyrdom in that age. Among this noble company are celebrated Gregory of Alexandria, Eusebius, Nectarius, Zeno, Basil, Ancyranus, Cyril of Jerusalem, and others. In the city of Egypt, several honourable virgins were led naked into the theatre, then cut open, filled with oats and barley, and thrown to the pigs to be torn apart.

units.la: XXXII. Persequutiones, quas Ecclesiæ Dei intentârunt Impp. Romani, sequutæ sunt PONTIFICVM ROMANORVM: quib. aliquot retrò seculis, auxilio Regum & Principum, Ecclesiam infestârunt. Harum fuere perplures. In præcipuis numerantur illæ in Petrum Valdum, Iohannem Viclefum, Iohannem Huffum, Hieronymum Pragensem, Hieronymam Savanorolam & pios eorum assectas, in flammatæ atq; exercitatæ ab anno MCLXX. usq; ad annum MDXXX. a quo tempore, postquam salvifica Evangelii lux ex profundo tenebrarum fundo emersit, innumeræ ad hanc diem persequutiones accidere.
units.tr: XXXII. The persecutions that the Roman emperors launched against the Church of God were followed by those of the Roman POPES, who in several past centuries attacked the Church with the help of kings and princes. There were very many of these. Among the chief are those against Peter Waldo, John Wycliffe, John Hus, Jerome of Prague, Jerome Savonarola and their pious followers, which were kindled and carried on from the year 1170 to the year 1530. From that time, after the saving light of the Gospel had risen out of the deep darkness, countless persecutions have occurred down to the present day.

units.la: XXXIII. Notæ sunt in orthodoxos Gallos exercitatæ diversis locis: nominatim Meti, Meldæ, apud Lingones & Cadurcos, Andegavi, Ambasiæ, Vassij, Carcassone, Velaunoduri, Augustonemeti, Castroduni, Divione, Blæsis, Torusij, Pictavij, Rotomagi: ubi clarissimus vir, Augustinus Marloratus, ante Mariæ templum suspensus truncatus, & caput ejus supra pontem palo affixum fuit.
units.tr: XXXIII. Persecutions against the orthodox in France are well known, carried out in various places, namely at Metz, Meaux, among the Lingones and the Cadurci, at Angers, Amboise, Vassy, Carcassonne, Velaunodurum, Augustonemetum, Châteaudun, Dijon, Blois, Tour, Poitiers, and Rouen. There the most illustrious man, Augustin Marlorat, was hanged before the church of Mary, beheaded, and his head was fixed on a stake above the bridge.

units.la: XXXIIII. Notæ sunt etiam Merindoliana & Cabrariensis in Provincia; quæ accidit anno MDXLIII. & V. Araufiensis; quæ anno MDLXII. Parisina, Trojana, Aureliana, Bituricensis, Tolosana, & Burdegalensis; quæ accidere anno MDLXXII. infausti illâ Sambartolomaei die, & seqq. in quibus locis sancti Martyres alii suspensi, alii exusti, alii lapidibus obruti, alii præcipites dati, alii submersi, nonnulli exsecti, dissecti, confossi, suffossi, cæsi, concîsi, atque aliis immanissimis supplicis mactati fuerunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. Also well known are the massacres at Mérindol and Cabrières in Provence, which took place in 1543, and the one at Orange in 1562; and the ones at Paris, Troyes, Orléans, Bourges, Toulouse, and Bordeaux, which happened in 1572 on that unlucky day of St Bartholomew and the days following. In these places holy martyrs were variously hanged, burned, stoned, thrown headlong, drowned, some were cut up, dissected, pierced through, buried alive, beaten, hacked to pieces, and put to death with other most savage tortures.

units.la: XXXV. Silentio hîc prætereiri non debet illa in Araufienses postissimum exercitata crudelitas: quam augustissimus huius ævi historicus Augustus Thuanus his verbis elegantibus, sed patheticis describit, quum inquit: Victor hostis nullo non immanitatis genere in eos, qui in urbe remanserant, sævit. Nam qui primum impetum effugêre, alii lentis ac minutis pugionum ictibus, sic, ut se mori sentirent, occisi: alii supra contos, sarissas ac strictos enses præcipitati: alii ad cremisterum [?] paxillos appensi & combusti: alii deniq; exsecti, nec decrepitis senibus mutilatis, & in lecto per valetudinaria decumbentibus ægris miserúq;, messoribus, subitâ obsessione in urbe oppressis, quibus nulla præter falces arma, parcitum: pleræq; fœminæ interfectæ: aliæ ad fenestras & porticus suspensæ, & avulsis ex earum amplexibus parvulis infantibus, scloppetorum ictibus confossæ: multæ virgines per vim corruptæ: pueri multi item rapti, & ad nefandam libidinem stiandam in miseram captivitatem; ex qua nonnisi diu post redierunt, abductî. Auxerunt crudelitatem contumeliosa spectacula pro ductis mulierum cadaveribus, & in earum pudenda boum cornibus & saxis ac stipitibus ad ludibrium injectis. Virorum item interfectorum plagæ foliis sacrorum librorum farctæ, qui ut vernaculâ lingua scripti ab illi discerpti passim jacebant. Nec adversa factio, quæ hosti ad oppidum capiendum, prodita concivium salute, viam straverat, furorem evasit: nam quum se in platea armati cum uxoribus ac pueris conglobâssen, hostes eos ad defensionem se parare rati, irruunt; & ad unum omnes [?] rucidant: nec proinde illi civium suorū exitio diu lætati sunt. Inde d[?]arcem itum, cujus præsidiarij vita pasti, ad unum omnes, qui CIX. [?]umerati sunt, aut præcipitati, aut gladio deleti sunt, exundate passim per urbe cruore: post cædeis in domos incendiis sævitū, publicæ ædes srpetibus flammis, etiâ Episcopi palatiû absumptû est, & CCC. privatorum domus, in isq; plæriq;, qui latebant, præfocati: vixq; exoratis post ingentia tonitrua insolitis imbribus incendium restingui potuit; qua commoditate usi plerique, qui a strage superabant per noctem aufugiunt, & ad socios, qui Seriniani substiterant, se conferunt: tum direptae ae-des, quibus ignis pepercerat, ac postridie moenia, Serbelloni jussu, a fundamentis eversa. Haec Thuanus: ex quibus, tanquam ex ungue leonem, persequutorum Evangelii efferatum animum, & plus quàm Phalaricum cognoscere nobis liceat.
units.tr: XXXV. Here that cruelty practised especially against the people of Orange must not be passed over in silence. The most august historian of this age, Augustus Thuanus, describes it in elegant yet moving words, when he says: The victorious enemy raged against those who had remained in the city with every kind of savagery. Those who escaped the first onslaught were killed, some by slow and small stabs of daggers, so that they felt themselves dying; others were thrown down upon pikes, lances and drawn swords; others were hung on stakes and burned; others, finally, were cut to pieces. Old men, who were decrepit and maimed, and sick people lying in bed in the infirmaries, were spared neither; reapers, overwhelmed in the city by a sudden siege, had no weapons except their sickles; most of the women were killed; others were hanged at the windows and porticoes, and small infants were torn from their embraces and pierced by gunshots; many virgins were violently ravished; many boys likewise were seized and led away into miserable captivity to satisfy unspeakable lust, and they returned only long afterwards. The cruelty was increased by insulting displays: the corpses of women were dragged about, and in their private parts were thrust horns of oxen, stones and stakes, for mockery. The wounds of the slain men were stuffed with the leaves of the sacred books, which, since they were written in the vernacular, were torn up and lay scattered everywhere. Nor did the hostile faction, which had betrayed the safety of its fellow citizens and paved the way for the enemy to take the town, escape the fury: for when they had gathered armed in the square with their wives and children, the enemy, thinking they were preparing to defend themselves, rushed in and butchered them all to a man. Nor did the enemy rejoice long at the destruction of their own citizens. Then they went to the citadel, whose garrison had been fed on the promise of their lives; all who were counted, 109 in number, were either thrown down or put to the sword, and blood ran everywhere through the city. After the slaughter, they raged with fires against the houses; the public buildings were consumed by the greedy flames, even the bishop's palace was destroyed, and the houses of 300 private citizens, in which many who were hiding were suffocated. Scarcely after great thunder and unusual rains could the fire be quenched. Most of those who survived the massacre used this opportunity to flee through the night and join their allies who had stopped at Serignan. Then the houses that the fire had spared were plundered, and the next day the walls were razed to the ground at the order of Serbelloni. Thus Thuanus. From these accounts, as one might know a lion from its claw, we may recognise the fierce spirit of the persecutors of the Gospel, more than Phalaris.

units.la: XXXVI. Quantam heu! barbariè in Parisinâ laniena unius Co-linius, Galliae admiralius, expertus sit, horrendum est dictu. Quùm fortis ille Heros in cubili suo gladio interemtus è fenestrâ praecipitatus esset cadaver ejus miris modis injuriosè foedatum, in stabulum proximum abjectum, & postremò capite, quod Romam usque perlatum, velut Ecclesiae ejus trophaeum, pudendis item & manibus ac pedibus trun-catis, per vicos ad Sequanae ripam tractum fuit: ubi aliquot dies spe-ctantium libidini, multorum etiam justa indignatione, qui rabiem illam Regi & Galliae in posterum magno constituram augurabantur, prostabat. Multas myriades trucidatorum aliorum sileo: è quorum id temporis pretioso sanguine valida Galliae flumina, Rhodanus, Se-quana, Ligeris, Garumna, hinc inde rubebant.
units.tr: XXXVI. What barbarity Coligny, the admiral of France, suffered in the Parisian slaughter is horrible to relate. When that brave hero had been killed with a sword in his bedroom and thrown from the window, his corpse was shamefully and outrageously defiled. It was dragged into the nearby stable, and then his head was cut off and carried all the way to Rome as a trophy of his Church. His genitals, hands and feet were also cut off, and his body was dragged through the streets to the bank of the Seine. There it lay for several days, exposed to the lust of spectators and to the righteous indignation of many who foretold that this fury would bring great trouble to the King and to France in future. I pass over the many myriads of others who were butchered. From their precious blood the mighty rivers of France, the Rhône, the Seine, the Loire and the Garonne, were reddened here and there.

units.la: XXXVII. Quàm miserabilis strages fidelium etiam extra Galliam, iisdem annis, maximè ab anno MDXLII. quo Tri-dentinum Concilium à Pontifice Rom. ad KL. Novemb. indictum fuerat, sit edita: testantur martyrologia ecclesiarum Anglicarum, Bel-gicarum, Hispanicarum praesertim Hispalensis, Italicarum praesertim regni Neapolitani, Pedemontanarum praesertim Saluziensis, Lotha-ringicarum et Germanicarum Smalcadici praesertim belli tempore: in quibus utriusque sexus homines, regio orti stemmate, doctrinâ, virtute & dignitate praestantes, & in unâ quidem Angliâ uno biennio supra octingentos, occubuêre: interq; alios Iohanna Graja Angliae haeres, Thomas Cranmerus Angliae Archiepiscopus & primas, Iohannes Hopperus Episcopus Glocestriae, Nicolaus Ridleus Episcopus Londini, Hugo Latimerus Episcopus Vorcestriae, Iohannes Aegidius, Constantius Fontius canonici et doctores Hispalenses, Iohannes Diazius, Ludoicus Pascalis, & alii principes viri: in quibus Martinus Bucerus, & Paulus Fagius, in Angliâ Professores, ante quadriennium mortui, effosi combustiq; sunt.
units.tr: XXXVII. How wretched the slaughter of the faithful was outside France in the same years, especially from the year 1542, when the Roman Pontiff announced the Council of Trent for the Kalends of November, is attested by the martyrologies of the English, Belgian and especially Spanish churches, above all that of Seville, and of the Italian churches, especially the kingdom of Naples, of the Piedmontese churches, especially Saluzzo, and of the Lorraine and German churches, especially during the Schmalkaldic war. In these, men and women of both sexes, distinguished by royal birth, learning, virtue and rank, perished. In England alone, over eight hundred died in a single two-year period. Among others were Joan Gray, heir of England; Thomas Cranmer, archbishop and primate of England; John Hooper, bishop of Gloucester; Nicholas Ridley, bishop of London; Hugh Latimer, bishop of Worcester; John Egidius, Constantius Fontius, canons and teachers of Seville; John Diaz, Louis Pascal, and other leading men. Among them, Martin Bucer and Paul Fagius, professors in England who had died four years earlier, were dug up and burned.

units.la: XXXVIII. Referunt non sine miseratione annales Belgici, furiatum tyrannum, Albæ Ducem, plane exutâ fronte gloriari au-sum, se tẽpore administrationis suæ Belgicæ octodecim millia Evan-gelicorum carnificis manu necanda procurasse: facinore inaudito, quodq; solum probavit qui commisit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The Belgian annals report, not without pity, that the raging tyrant, the Duke of Alva, boasted with a brazen face that during his governorship of the Netherlands he had caused eighteen thousand Evangelicals to be put to death by the executioner's hand. It was an unheard-of deed, which only the one who committed it approved.

units.la: XXXIX. Persequutiones, quas Ecclesiæ non tantùm in Carinthiâ, Styriâ & Austriâ, sed etiam in Bohemiâ, Moraviâ, Silesiâ, Lusatiâ, Ungariâ, & locis aliis vicinis, Palatinatu item superiore & inferiore, his ultimis annis passæ sunt, nemo enarret, nisi
units.tr: XXXIX. No one could recount the persecutions which the Church has suffered in recent years, not only in Carinthia, Styria and Austria, but also in Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia, Lusatia, Hungary and other neighbouring places, as well as in the Upper and Lower Palatinate, except

units.la: Cui linguæ centum sint oráque centum.
units.tr: Though he had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths,

units.la: Fumant adhuc urbes eversæ: oppida, arces, monasteria acervus sepulta jacent: pagi viduati colonis laceri sunt aut exusti: agri squalent inarati atque frequentibus populatibus horrent: ne sylvis quidem melius est, ut quæ tædiu [?] manent aut in frondes: nusquam culturæ honos, ne mentio quidem ulla aut memoria: mœstos locos & solitudini relictos infelices insident aves, quib. non aliunde pabulū, quàm exstrage corporum, partim ferro, partim frigore interemtorum: ossa, quæ omnis semper Religio contexit, quæ pietas non sustinet videre, dissipantur, confringuntur, proteruntur. Eccui ferae, obsecro, sua feritas tam pertinax, sua saevitia tam inexplebilis, ut suis vulneribus delectetur? ut propriis manibus hæc laxet & laceret? At enim Religionis orthodoxæ persequutorum saevitia irrorata cruore humano, prodigiosa ista crimina progignit, quorum nec dum prob dolor! est finis.
units.tr: The cities overthrown are still smoking; towns, citadels and monasteries lie buried in heaps; villages stripped of their inhabitants lie torn or burned; fields lie neglected and unploughed, bristling with repeated devastations. Not even the woods fare better, for such trees as remain are either bare or in leaf. Nowhere is there any honour of cultivation, not even a mention or memory of it. Unhappy birds haunt these sad places, abandoned to desolation, and find their food nowhere but in the corpses of those killed partly by the sword and partly by cold. The bones, which every religion has always covered, and which piety cannot bear to see, are scattered, broken and trampled underfoot. To what beast, I beg you, is its savagery so persistent, its cruelty so insatiable, that it delights in its own wounds, or tears and rends these with its own hands? Yet the cruelty of the persecutors of orthodox religion, drenched in human blood, gives birth to these monstrous crimes, and alas, there is still no end to them.

units.la: XL. Nemini quin etiam ignota est atrox laniena, quæ in nobili Rætorum provincia Valtelinâ plane barbarum in modum, circa sesqui modo annū exercitata fuit: in qua Evangelii professores omnis ætatis, sexūs & conditionis, nullo aut fidei datæ, aut locorum sacrorū, ubi precibus operam dabant, respectu, à Pontificiis incolis, etiam ipsis met propinquis ac fratribus, magno numero, partim ferro, plumbo, igne, aquis & lapidibus, ut oviculæ à laniis, mactati, trajecti, exusti, suffocati & collisi, partim triste in exilium, asperas per alpes, pulsi dissipatiq; sunt: lamentabili ad modum spectaculo, quum per avia senes pueris mixti incedere, & mulieres in cunis inter brachia, in sinu denique infantes ejulantes gestare, ædes etiam dirui, & ossa multorum humo effossa inflammari conspiceretur, et ne quidē summis Magistratibus parceretur, tantâ perduellione, & tantâ saevitiâ, quantam sera posteritas haud credet, aut si credat, plenùs deflebit lacrymis, detestabi-tur & abominabitur.
units.tr: XL. Indeed, no one is unaware of the savage slaughter which, in the noble Rhaetian province of the Valtellina, was carried out in a thoroughly barbarous manner for about a year and a half. In it, professors of the Gospel of every age, sex and condition, with no regard to any pledge given or to the sacred places where they gave themselves to prayer, were in great numbers slaughtered, pierced, burned, suffocated and crushed by Papist inhabitants, even by their own relatives and brothers. Some were struck down with iron, lead, fire, water and stones, like sheep by butchers; others were driven into miserable exile over rough Alpine paths, scattered and dispersed. It was a pitiable spectacle: old men walked through the wilds mixed with boys, women carried infants in their cradles and in their arms, and even children wailed in their bosoms. Houses were also torn down, and the bones of many were dug out of the ground and set on fire. Not even the highest magistrates were spared. Such treachery and such cruelty, as late posterity will hardly believe, or if it believes, will lament with full tears, detest and abominate.

units.la: XLI. Quid Ratis ipsis, Valtelinae dominus, perpaucos ante menses acciderit, hodieq; accidat: notius est, quàm ut longâ commemoratione indigeat. Hic victor hostis cùm in alios innocuos homines, qui domi remanserant, tum verò atque imprimis in aliquos verbi ministros nullo non crudelitatis genere est usus, ut partim spoliatis, partim in vincula detrusis, partim denique arduos per montes fugatis dissipatis, et penè nū[?] frigore famèq; enectis, postquam templa hinc inde, cathedras & subsellia eorum vastavit, diruit, conspurcavit, idololatrico cultu in illa ocyus introducto.
units.tr: XLI. What happened to the Grisons themselves, lords of the Valtellina, a few months ago, and is happening even today, is too well known to need a long account. This victorious enemy used every kind of cruelty against other innocent men who had remained at home, and above all against certain ministers of the Word. Some he despoiled, some he thrust into chains, and some, finally, he drove over the steep mountains, scattering them and nearly killing them with cold and hunger, half-naked. He laid waste, tore down and defiled their churches, their chairs and benches, and quickly introduced idolatrous worship into them.

units.la: XLII. Veterib. illus et recentib. persequutionibus annumerari debet Gallica hodierna, quae etiamnum durat: in qua orthodoxi Galli pluribus locis, per totum regnum, nominatim in Bearnensi provinciâ, Aquitaniâ, Pictaviâ, & alibi, coacervato undiq; ex omni loco et ordine, experientissimo milite regio, graves conflictationes ab ultimo biennio sustinuere: quib. alii oppressi, sub Antichristi jugo imos singultus ducunt: nonnulli veluti Montalbanenses, Rupellenses, & alii, Deo pro ipsis è coelo pugnante, hactenus superiores sunt facti, ingenti ipsorum solatio & gaudio: persequutorum verò indelebili nævo, & ineffabili clade: quippe horum quinquaginta circiter Principes, Mareschalli, Duces, Barones, & mille ac quingenti è primariâ nobilitate, et vicies circiter mille capitanei & gregarii milites partim ferro, partim lue absumti sunt: admirando & miraculoso exemplo auxilii Dei; qui etiamnum hodie populo suo, recti conscio, & precum memori, & manu animoq; forti, Gedeones suos ostendit, quibus auxiliantibus hostem feriant, & se suamq; religionem defendant, ut nosse discant, à Dei solius dextrâ victoriam stare & impetrari.
units.tr: XLII. The present French persecution, which still continues, should be counted among the old and recent persecutions. In it, orthodox Frenchmen throughout the whole kingdom, especially in the province of Béarn, in Aquitaine, Poitou and elsewhere, have for the last two years endured severe assaults from every place and rank, gathered from all sides by the royal soldiers, the most experienced of the army. Others have been crushed and sigh deep sighs under the yoke of Antichrist. Some, such as the people of Montauban and La Rochelle, with God fighting for them from heaven, have so far been made the victors, to their great comfort and joy, but to the persecutors an indelible stain and an unspeakable disaster. For about fifty of their princes, marshals, dukes and barons, fifteen hundred of the chief nobility, and about twenty thousand captains and common soldiers have been destroyed, some by the sword and some by plague.
