This is a wonderful and miraculous example of God's help, who even today shows his Gideons to his people, who are conscious of what is right, mindful of prayers, and strong of hand and spirit. With their help they strike the enemy and defend themselves and their religion, so that they may learn that victory stands and is obtained from the right hand of God alone.

units.la: XLIII. Memorabilis hîc est beati Martyris Danielis Chamierii virtus, cujus operâ grande Bellarmini opus totum prostratum, mox luci commissum videbimus. Is durante Montalbanensis civitatis, cujus id temporis pastor erat, obsidione, magnos spiritus nō hortãdo tantùm gessit, sed pugnãdo etiã inter certãtes cùm viros, tum mulieres (quae et ipsae hîc amplam laudem retulerunt) concitavit, adurbis moenia, ferreos inter imbres, stans intrepidus, licet elucente tormentis flam-mâ coelum ac solum mugire audiret: licet moenia ipsa iteratos per bombos tenuati, milites conscendere, & pedes inferre, tubis tym-panisque omnia perstrepere, pugnantes clamare, morientes fremere videret: donec ipse pro lege & grege, pro aris & focis, tormenti majo-rus illatus, fortiter occubuit, triumphalis martyrii coronam con-sequutus.
units.tr: XLIII. The virtue of the blessed martyr Daniel Chamier is worth remembering; through his work we shall see the great work of Bellarmine totally overthrown and soon published. While Montauban, of which he was then pastor, was under siege, he not only inspired great courage by his exhortations, but also by fighting himself, he stirred up among the combatants both men and women (who also won ample praise here). Standing fearless before the walls amid iron showers, he heard the sky and the ground roar while the flame of the artillery shone. He saw the walls themselves thinned by repeated bombardment, soldiers climbing up and bringing their feet forward, everything resounding with trumpets and drums, the fighters shouting and the dying groaning. At last, for law and flock, for altars and hearths, a greater torment was inflicted on him, and he fell bravely, obtaining the crown of triumphant martyrdom.

units.la: XLIV. CAETERUM has atq; alias graves persequutiones cur Deus Ecclesiæ Christianæ, charissimæ sponsæ suæ, quæ pupilla oculi ipsius est, immiserit, non injuria piæ mentes quærere solet. Hic causæ cur id faciat, sunt perplures ac graves; & præcipuæ quidem istæ:
units.tr: XLIV. Why God has sent these and other grave persecutions upon the Christian Church, his dearest bride, who is the apple of his eye, pious minds are wont to ask, and not without reason. There are very many weighty reasons why he does so, and the chief of these are the following:

units.la: XLV. Prima: quia Deus vult ejusmodi persequutionib. declara-re gloriam, potentiam ac majestatem suam: quòd nempe ceu fidelis noster conditor & possit & velit in medio persequutionum æstu nos tueri servare ac liberare. Et quanquam non semper tuta præstat corpora, sed illa sæpe à Tyrannis affligi atq; occidi sinit: tamen semper confirmat fidelium suorum animos, ut intrepidè ac fortiter cruciatus corporis perferant ac vincant. quod non tantùm veteris ævi historia Esdræ, Estheræ, Danielis, Macchabæorum & aliorum, sed etiam ævi posterioris & hodierna clarissimè testatur: ex qua divinas ejusmodi et miraculosas conservationes omninò plures accidisse constat. Hoc Paulus docet, quum inquit, Fidelis autem est Deus, qui non sinet vos tentari supra id, quod potestis, sed unà cum tentatione præstabit etiam exitum, ut possitis sufferre, 1. Cor. 10,13, Item, In omnibus premimur, at non coarctamur: hæsitamus, at nō prorsus hæremus: persequutionem patimur, sed in eā non deserimur: deiicimur, at non perimus, 2. Cor. 4,8.9.
units.tr: XLV. First: because God wishes by such persecutions to display his glory, power and majesty, namely that as our faithful Creator he both can and will protect and save us in the heat of persecution. And although he does not always grant bodies safety, but often allows them to be afflicted and killed by tyrants, he always strengthens the minds of his faithful, so that they may bear and overcome bodily torments with courage and fortitude. This is clearly attested not only by the history of ancient times, of Ezra, Esther, Daniel, the Maccabees and others, but also by later times and our own, from which it is established that such divine and miraculous preservations have happened very many times. Paul teaches this when he says: "God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it" (1 Cor. 10:13). Likewise: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed" (2 Cor. 4:8–9).

units.la: XLVI. Altera: quia Deo visum est persequutionibus patefacere hominib. veritatem verbi sui. Fit enim, ut fideles in vincula detrusi, capti atq; in judicia pertracti illam aperte ac liberè cõfiteantur: ut pro ara & puppim salutis suæ faciant unicum & perfectissimū meritum DN.N.I.CHRISTI, post habitis meritis, satisfactionib. et operib. humanis, sacrificio Missæ, religioso imaginum cultu, peregrinationi-bus ad imagines, intercessionib. Sanctorum, igne purgatorio, & aliis cerebri humani putidis commentis & superstitionib. vanis ac impiis infinitis: quibus hodie in Papatu magnâ religione ad placandum Deum, & promerendum peccatorum veniam vacatur.
units.tr: XLVI. The second reason: because God has willed, through persecutions, to make the truth of his word known to men. For it happens that the faithful, thrown into chains, seized, and dragged before the courts, openly and freely confess it, so that they make the one and most perfect merit of our Lord Jesus Christ their sole refuge and anchor of salvation, after setting aside merits, satisfactions and human works, the sacrifice of the Mass, the religious worship of images, pilgrimages to images, the intercession of the saints, purgatorial fire, and the countless other putrid fictions of the human brain and vain and impious superstitions, by which today in the Papacy men seek, with great devotion, to appease God and earn forgiveness of sins.

units.la: XLVII. Tertia: quia Deo placet justo judicio, sed tamē paterno fideles suos ob peccata, quib. ipsi quoq; sunt obnoxii, punire et castigare, sicq; ad resipiscentiā eos vocare. Hac de causā Deus Iudæos Babylonių, Chaldæis aliisq; tyrannis affligendos quondam permisit: & hinc beatus martyr Cyprianus testatur, causam persequutionis sui temporis fuisse fidelium vitam dissolutiorem. Similem indicat Eusebius, persequutionem sub Diocletiano describens: innuens, emolumento fidelium fieri, si ipsi persequutionum mole premantur. quod Paulus pariter docet, quum inquit, Sed quum judicamur, à Domino castigamur, ne cum Mundo condemnemur, 1. Cor. 11.32.
units.tr: XLVII. The third reason: because God, with a just but nonetheless fatherly judgment, is pleased to punish and chastise his faithful for their sins, to which they too are liable, and so to call them to repentance. For this reason God once allowed the Jews to be afflicted by the Babylonians, the Chaldeans and other tyrants; and hence the blessed martyr Cyprian testifies that the cause of the persecution of his own time was the more dissolute life of the faithful. Eusebius, describing the persecution under Diocletian, indicates a similar cause, implying that it turns to the advantage of the faithful if they are oppressed by the weight of persecutions. Paul likewise teaches this when he says: "But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor. 11:32).

units.la: XLVIII. Quarta: quia Deus persequutionib. vult probare fidem nostram, et experiri, an illa sit sincera, firma & constans: sicut aurifices aurum & argentum probant & purgant igne. Huc respicit Petrus, inquiens, Charissimi, ne tanquam hospites, exploratione illa per ignem, quæ fit in nobis ad vestri experimentum, percellimini, ut si peregrinum aliquid vobis accideret. Imò ineo, quod consortes estis afflictionum Christi gaudete, ut & quum patefiet ejus gloria, gaudeatis exultantes: puta Apostolorum ipsorum met exemplo, qui persequutionem passi à primoribus Hierosolymitanis, abierunt gaudentes, quod digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine Iesu contumeliā afficerentur, 1. Pet. 4, 12, 13. Actor. 5, 21.
units.tr: XLVIII. The fourth reason: because God wishes by persecutions to test our faith and to try whether it is sincere, firm and constant, just as goldsmiths test and purify gold and silver with fire. Peter has this in view when he says: "Beloved, do not be dismayed by the fiery trial which comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share in Christ's sufferings, so that when his glory is revealed you may rejoice and exult" (think of the very example of the Apostles themselves, who, when persecuted by the leaders of Jerusalem, went away rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus: 1 Pet. 4:12, 13; Acts 5:21).

units.la: XLIX. Quinta: quia Deus persequutionibus, quibus exercet fideles, significare vult, quid exspectandum sit infidelibus, nempe longe gravius & truculentius judicium: idque non in hac tantum vita, sed etiam post eam in exitio æterno. Etenim si in virenti ligno ista accidūt, in arido quid fiet? inquit Dominus. Et eodē illo loco Petrus, Tempus est, ut incipiat judicium à domo Dei: quòd si primum incipit à nobis, quis erit finis eorum, qui non parent Evangelio? Et si justus vix servatur: impius & peccator ubi comparabit? Confer quæ Daniel scribit de severo judicio exercendo à Deo in bestias, hoc est, persequutores Ecclesiæ, cap. 7. v. 9. & seqq.
units.tr: XLIX. The fifth reason: because by the persecutions with which God afflicts the faithful he wishes to signify what is to be expected by unbelievers, namely a far heavier and more savage judgment, and this not only in this life but also after it, in eternal destruction. For the Lord says: "If these things happen to the green wood, what will happen to the dry?" And in the same place Peter says: "It is time for judgment to begin with the house of God; and if it begins with us first, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" Compare what Daniel writes of the severe judgment to be exercised by God upon the beasts, that is, the persecutors of the Church, ch. 7, v. 9 and following.

units.la: L. Alias rationes brevitatis causā omittimus. Ut vero persequutiones æquo animo ferant homines fideles: & jam commemorata cautiones, & subsequentes, stimulo magno eis esse possunt ac debent.
units.tr: L. For the sake of brevity we omit other reasons. But so that the faithful may bear persecutions with an equal mind, the cautions already mentioned and those that follow can and ought to serve them as a great spur.

units.la: LI. Etenim quotquot persequutiones ob confessionem Evangelii patiuntur, certò norunt, se consortes fieri persequutionum Christi, Servatoris sui: ut qui eadem de causā captus, casus, acerbissimis contumeliis[?] exceptus, ludibrio habitus, flagris cruentatus, spinis coronatus, in crucem actus, vulneribus concisus & occisus fuit. Perhonorificum autem est, conformari capiti, magistro ac domino suo. Hoc argumento Christus ipse Apostolos suos est consolatus, Si mundus vos odit, scitis, me prius, quam vos, illis odio habitum, Iohan.15, 18,19,20.
units.tr: LI. For whoever suffers persecution for the confession of the gospel knows for certain that he becomes a partner in the persecutions of Christ, his Saviour: who, taken for the same cause, bound, accused with the most bitter insults, mocked, torn with scourges, crowned with thorns, led to the cross, pierced with wounds and put to death. Indeed it is most honourable to be conformed to the head, teacher and lord. With this argument Christ himself consoled his Apostles: "If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you" (John 15:18, 19, 20).

units.la: LII. Deinde certi sunt, si constanter tulerint & pertulerint persequutiones atque ita communicaverint cum perpessionib. Christi: ipsos consortes quoque futuros gloriae Christi & gaudiorum caelestium. Idem tradit Paulus, inquiens, Cum eo patimur, ut cum eo etiam glorificemur, Rom.8,17. item, Si toleramus, etiam cum eo regnabimus, 2. Tim.2,11,12.
units.tr: LII. Next, they are certain that if they bear persecutions steadfastly and endure them, and so share in the sufferings of Christ, they will also become partners in the glory of Christ and in heavenly joys. Paul likewise teaches this, saying: "We suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him" (Rom. 8:17); and again: "If we endure, we shall also reign with him" (2 Tim. 2:11, 12).

units.la: LIII. Praterea sciunt, quum patienter ferunt probra Mundi propter nomen Christi: id ipsis cedere in gloriam ac salutem: ut quod iudicio sit, requiescere super ipsos spiritum Dei. Etenim homo carnalis pronus est ad probra non ferendum, sed regerendum. Id non tantum Petrus loco citato ostendit, quum inquit, Si probris afficimini ob nomen Christi, beati estis: quoniam ille gloriae & ille Dei Spiritus super vos requiescit: sed etiam Dominus ipse beatos nos pronunciat, quum propter justitiam convitiis proscindimur, mendaciis obruimur, & injuriis dilaceramur.
units.tr: LIII. Moreover, they know that when they patiently bear the reproaches of the world for the name of Christ, these turn to their glory and salvation, and that the Spirit of God rests upon them. For carnal man is inclined not to bear reproaches but to return them. Peter shows this not only in the passage cited, when he says: "If you are reviled for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you"; but the Lord himself also pronounces us blessed when for righteousness' sake we are cut down with insults, overwhelmed with lies and torn apart with injuries.

units.la: LIV. Persuasi sunt etiam sub crucegementes[?], Deum, tanquam justum judicem, innocentiam suam suo tempore asserturum: quum videlicet puniet persequutores in hac vita, & post eam: juxta gravissimam sententiam Apostoli, Iustum est apud Deum vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem, 2. Thess.1,5.
units.tr: LIV. Those who groan under the cross are also persuaded that God, as a just judge, will vindicate their innocence in his own time, namely when he punishes their persecutors in this life and after it, according to the weighty sentence of the Apostle: "It is just with God to repay with affliction those who afflict you" (2 Thess. 1:5).

units.la: LV. Et certè si historias cum veteres, tum recentes pervolvimus: manifestè deprehendimus, persequutores populi Dei plurimùm horrendis poenis è medio sublatos esse.
units.tr: LV. And certainly, if we turn over both ancient and recent histories, we clearly find that the persecutors of the people of God have for the most part been removed by dreadful punishments.

units.la: LVI. Pharao, rex Aegypti, quo tyrannum truculentiorem Sol non vidit, postquam Hebraeos dirum in modum diu vexâsset, tandem cum potentissimo exercitu suo, in mari rubro miserè periit. Achab, rex Israelis, in bello cōtra Syros telo percussus, & Iezabel uxor ejus è fenestra praeceps data, equo conculcata & canibus dilanianda projecta fuit. Assyriis & Chaldaeis septies Deus rependit, illos faciens tetrum spectaculum Mundi totius. Antiochus, rex Syriae, insanabili percussus plagâ, ex quâ saevus viscerum dolor eum comprehenderat, arru gestatorio delapsus, isto casu adeo affectus est, ut vermes ex corpore ipsius scaturirent, & teter putredinis ejus odor toti exercitui gravis esset, sic, ut à nemine amplius gestari posset.
units.tr: LVI. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, than whom the sun has never seen a more savage tyrant, after he had long vexed the Hebrews in a dreadful manner, at last perished wretchedly in the Red Sea with his most powerful army. Ahab, king of Israel, struck by an arrow in war against the Syrians, and his wife Jezebel, thrown headlong from a window, was trampled by a horse and cast out to be torn by dogs. God repaid the Assyrians and Chaldeans seven times over, making them a loathsome spectacle to the whole world. Antiochus, king of Syria, struck by an incurable plague from which a savage pain in his bowels had seized him, fell from his travelling chariot, and was so afflicted by this accident that worms swarmed out of his body, and the foul stench of his putrefaction was so grievous to the whole army that no one could carry him any longer.

units.la: LVII. Herodes Magnus paulò post crudele infanticidium saevissimis morbis excarnificatus interiit Hierichunte, agitantibus & inquietantibus illum ultricibus furiis, & divinâ Nemesi ad supplicia raptante. Herodes Antipas novennio post jugulatum Iohannem Baptistam, unâ cum Herodiade pudendum subivit exilium. Herodes Agrippa à vermibus erosus concidit. Pilatus in multas incidens ca-lamitates manu suâ se interfecit Vienna in Gallia, quò in faedum exilium relegatus erat, septennio à morte Domini, quem ipse morti insontem adjudicaverat. Et Iudaeorum infelix natio universa nondum exsatiata fuit caede servorum Dei, quum grave judicium est experta, gladio & fame peremtis undecies centenis millib. & centenis millibus venditis.
units.tr: LVII. Herod the Great, shortly after the cruel slaughter of the infants, died at Jericho, worn away by most savage diseases, with avenging furies harassing and troubling him, and divine Nemesis hurrying him to punishment. Herod Antipas, nine years after he had beheaded John the Baptist, underwent shameful exile together with Herodias. Herod Agrippa was eaten by worms and fell. Pilate, falling into many calamities, killed himself with his own hand at Vienne in Gaul, to which he had been banished into miserable exile seven years after the death of the Lord, whom he himself had condemned to death though innocent. And the unhappy Jewish nation as a whole, not yet satiated with the slaughter of the servants of God, has experienced a grievous judgment: 1,100,000 slain by the sword and famine, and 100,000 sold into slavery.

units.la: LVIII. Nero sibimet mortem conscivit gladio, qui Christianos gladio persequebatur, quo tempore tricies mille homines peste occubuêre Romae, & atrox civile bellum non multò post plura alia Romanorum millia absorpsit. Domitianus ut exitum suâ in Christianos saevitiâ dignum sortiretur, à propriis suis libertis interfectus est, & absque honore, aut cujusquam mœrore sepultus, imaginibus & statuis ejus à Senatu Rom. ubique abolitis extremo cum decore. Traianus in manibus suis persequutionib. vindic[?]am Dei in Rom. Imperium adeo concitavit, ut Tiberis aquis auctus Romam inundârit totam, inaesti-mabili damno domorum ac bonorum. Aurea domus Neronis subitò tunc conflagravit: Pantheon fulmine tactum & ipsum totum cum idolis est absumtum: terraemotu vehementi id temporis corruêre quatuor in Asiâ urbes, duae insignes in Graciâ, tres in Galatiâ, periitque funditus Antiochia, horribiliter per universum Imperium dominantibus fame & peste. quod et Antonini & Veri temporib. accidisse constat. Valerianus à Sapore, rege Persarum, victus & captus in carcere mansit ad senectam: unde emissus non est nisi quum regi equū conscensuro, pro scabello se substernere cogebatur. Aurelianus à suis confossus occidit. Diocletian[?] jam senex in horribili desperatione veneno hausto necavit semetipse. Maximianus, ejus in affligendis Christianis socius, à Constantino Massiliae obsessus, captus & suspensus est: ac in Tiberim juxta ponte Milvium precipitatus et submersus Maxentius Maximiani filius. Julianus apostata ingente exercitum ducturus in Persas, eo animo, ut illis domitis deinceps Christianos exstirparet, telo, quod nemo vidit unde venerit, in latere percussus interiit, quum sanguinem e vulnere manu accipiens, & in coelum spargens desperabundus dixisset, Νενίχηκας [?] Γαλιλαῖε, Vicisti Galilae, Christum contumeliose intelligens. Valens haeresi Arianorum addictus, & orthodoxorum persequutor acerrimus, in bello contra Gothos, caesus exercitu, telo itidem percussus est, & quum in casam quandam confugisset, ab insequente hoste una cum casa exustus. Phocas, qui Mauritium Imp. cum quinque filiis & Petro fratre occidit, victus in portu Constantinopolitano a Prisco genero suo, Heraciano & Photio, cujus ille uxorem vi construpaverat, quum in regiam confugisset, solio deturbatus, purpura spoliatus est, adq; Heraclium Imp. deductus, qui confestim ei jussit amputari manus, pedes, pudenda & caput, trunco reliquo combusto a militibus in foro, &c.
units.tr: LVIII. Nero took his own life with a sword, he who had persecuted Christians with the sword; at that time 30,000 men perished of plague at Rome, and a dreadful civil war not long afterwards swallowed up many more thousands of Romans. Domitian, so that he might meet an end worthy of his savagery against the Christians, was killed by his own freedmen, and was buried without honour or anyone's mourning, his images and statues everywhere abolished by the Roman Senate with the greatest disgrace. Trajan, by his persecutions, stirred up the vengeance of God upon the Roman Empire so that the Tiber, swollen with water, flooded all of Rome, with inestimable loss of houses and goods. The Golden House of Nero was suddenly burnt down at that time; the Pantheon, struck by lightning, was entirely consumed with its idols; in a violent earthquake of that time four cities in Asia, two notable ones in Greece and three in Galatia collapsed, and Antioch perished utterly, while famine and plague held sway horribly throughout the whole Empire. It is established that this also happened in the times of the Antonines and Verus. Valerian, conquered and captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, remained in prison into old age; he was released only when, as the king was about to mount his horse, he was forced to lie down as a footstool. Aurelian was stabbed to death by his own men. Diocletian, already old, in dreadful despair, drank poison and killed himself. Maximian, his partner in afflicting the Christians, was besieged at Marseilles by Constantine, captured and hanged, and thrown into the Tiber near the Milvian Bridge and drowned; Maxentius, son of Maximian. Julian the Apostate, about to lead a huge army against the Persians, intending, once they were subdued, to root out the Christians, was struck in the side by a weapon whose origin no one saw, and died; taking the blood from the wound in his hand and scattering it toward heaven, he said in despair: "Thou hast conquered, Galilean" [Νενίχηκας Γαλιλαῖε], meaning Christ in contempt. Valens, addicted to the Arian heresy and a most bitter persecutor of the orthodox, in war against the Goths, his army cut to pieces, was likewise struck by a weapon, and when he had fled into a certain hut, was burnt together with the hut by the pursuing enemy. Phocas, who had killed the Emperor Maurice together with his five sons and his brother Peter, was defeated in the harbour of Constantinople by his son-in-law Priscus, Heraclian and Photius, whose wife he had violently defiled; when he fled into the palace he was hurled from the throne and stripped of the purple, and was brought to Emperor Heraclius, who at once ordered his hands, feet, genitals and head to be cut off, and his remaining trunk to be burnt by the soldiers in the forum, etc.

units.la: LIX. Exempla integrorum populorum, veluti Vandalorum, Hunnorum, Gothorum, Saracenorum & aliorum, qui & ipsi Ecclesiam Dei dire exagitarunt, sed horrendas omnis generis poenas subivere, in medium afferri possent, sed horum commemoratione, ne nimis longum faciamus, supersedemus.
units.tr: LIX. Examples of whole peoples, such as the Vandals, Huns, Goths, Saracens and others who also savagely harassed the Church of God but underwent horrible punishments of every kind, could be brought forward; but, so as not to make this too long, we pass over their recollection.

units.la: LX. Quàm misero funestóque fato aliquot Pontifices Romani, qui posterioribus seculis fidem orthodoxam oppressam voluere, perempti sunt: historiae non sine horribili formidine testantur. Etenim plures illorum morbis antea inauditis oppressi sunt: aliqui mortui a suis inventi subito exspirarunt: quidam pulsi & capti: quidam veneno consumti sunt. Lucius II. a suis lapidibus obrutus: Lucius III. urbe ejectus, familia ejus caesa est: nonnullis oculi sunt eruti: alii conversa facie asinis impositi per urbem contumeliose circumducti. Hadrianus IV. suffocatus obiit. Johannes XXI. fornice subito ruente est oppressus. Johannem XII immanissimum & foedissimum monstrum, civis in adulterio uxoris suae deprehensu occidit. Bonifacium VIII. captivum Romam adduci curavit Philippus Pulcher, rex Gallia-rum: ubi intra dies XXXV. prae moerore exstinctus est: de quo exstat vulgatum, Intravit ut vulpes, regnavit ut leo, mortuus est ut canis. Platina, tanquam epiphonema historiae illius addit, dignum
units.tr: LX. The historians testify, not without dreadful alarm, how wretched and deadly a fate overtook those Roman Pontiffs in later centuries who wished the orthodox faith to be crushed. For many of them were overcome by diseases previously unheard of; some were found dead by their own people and died suddenly; some were driven out and captured; some were consumed by poison. Lucius II was buried under stones thrown by his own people. Lucius III was driven out of the city, and his family was slaughtered. Some had their eyes torn out; others were set facing backwards on asses and led shamefully through the city. Hadrian IV died by suffocation. John XXI was crushed when an arch suddenly collapsed. John XII, a most savage and foul monster, was killed by a husband who caught him in adultery with his wife. Philip the Fair, king of the French, had Boniface VIII brought to Rome as a captive; there, within thirty-five days, he died of grief. Concerning him there is the common saying: "He entered like a fox, reigned like a lion, and died like a dog." Platina, as a kind of epiphonema to that story, adds that it is worth

units.la: memoriâ: Hoc modo mortuus est Bonifacius ille, qui Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus, nationibus & populis, terrorem potiùs, quàm religionem, injicere conabatur: quique dare regna & auferre, pellere homines & reducere pro arbitrio animi conabatur, aurum undique conquisitum plus quàm dici potest sitiens, &c.
units.tr: remembering: "In this way died that Boniface who tried to strike terror rather than religion into emperors, kings, princes, nations and peoples; who tried, at the pleasure of his mind, to give kingdoms and take them away, to drive men out and bring them back, thirsting for gold sought out on every side more than can be said," and so on.

units.la: LXI. Portentosa classis Hispanica, quæ Dei ecclesiam in Angliâ, Scotiâ, Hibernia, Galliâ, Belgio et alibi subjugum Ibericum et leges Romanas coactura, ac quasi vivam absorptura erat, horrendum in Oceano interitum nemo est, qui nesciat. Hæc auspiciis Philippi II. regis Hispaniarum, totum fermè triennium apparata, navium militarium grandium centum quinquaginta, militibus veteranis ex Hispaniâ, Italiâ & aliunde collectis viginti mille, nautis decies mille, tormentis bis mille sexcentis quinquaginta, pyrio pulvere, globis & annonâ ad semestre instructissima, die XXVIII. Maji, ex portu Ulyssibonensi solvens, quum Angliam appetiisset, ab Anglis, Carolo Howardo thalassiarcho, & Francisco Draco prothalassiarcho, KL. Aug. & seqq. diebus, usque ad finem Aug. creberrimis incursionibus & conflictibus, sed maximè Deo è cœlis pugnante, labefactata, victa & profligata est, ingenti prædâ in potestatem serenissimæ Reginæ Elizabethæ redactâ. Digni sunt versus sequentes, qui de classis interitu huic loco inserantur: Straverat innumeris Hispanus navibus æquor, Regnis iuncturus sceptra Britanna suis. Tanti huius rogitas, quæ motus causa: feroces Movit in innocuos Christicolas Rabies. Impulit Ambitio gentem scelerata superbam, Et cupidos orbis vexit Avaritia. Quàm bene in innocuos grassandi efferbuit æstus, Milite Marrano funda petente maris: Quàm bene te, Ambitio mersit vanissima ventus Et tumidos tumidæ vos superastis aquæ: Quàm bene totius raptores orbis avaros Hausit inexhausti iusta vorago salis:
units.tr: LXI. The monstrous Spanish fleet, which was going to subjugate the Church of God in England, Scotland, Ireland, France, the Netherlands and elsewhere under the Iberian yoke and Roman laws, and was going to swallow it up as if alive, is known to everyone for its dreadful destruction at sea. It was prepared under the auspices of Philip II, king of Spain, over almost three years: one hundred and fifty large warships, twenty thousand veteran soldiers gathered from Spain, Italy and elsewhere, ten thousand sailors, two thousand six hundred and fifty guns, and gunpowder, shot and provisions for six months, most fully equipped. On 28 May it set sail from the port of Lisbon, and when it made for England, it was shaken, defeated and routed by the English under Charles Howard, admiral, and Francis Drake, vice-admiral, with the most frequent attacks and clashes on the first of August and the following days until the end of August, but above all by God fighting from heaven; a great booty was brought into the power of the most serene Queen Elizabeth. The following verses are worthy to be inserted here concerning the fleet's destruction: The Spaniard had covered the sea with countless ships, about to join to his own kingdoms the sceptres of Britain. You ask what was the cause of so great an undertaking: a fierce rage moved against innocent Christians. Ambition drove the proud nation to crime, and greed carried it on, eager for the world. How well the fever of raging against the innocent boiled up, when the Marrano soldier sought the sea by sling! How well, most empty Ambition, the wind sank you, and you, swollen waters, overcame the swelling ones! How well the vast whirlpool of the unexhausted sea swallowed the greedy plunderers of the whole world!

units.la: LXII. Decennio post anno nempe MDXCVIII. mense Septembri, ipse etiam classis hujusce architectus Philippus interiit, postquâ acutis humoribus corpus ejus horribili dolore diu jactatum fuit : qui quum nullis medicamentis abigi possent, aperto ad eos educendos corpore, ingens quotidie pediculorum copia, & pestilens pus effluxit, tanto foetore, ut praesentiam ejus nemo sustineret. Testis Ioh. Bouchier, oratione in laudem Philippi compositâ.
units.tr: LXII. Ten years later, namely in September 1598, Philip himself, the architect of this very fleet, died, after his body had long been tormented by sharp humours and horrible pain. Since these could not be driven away by any medicines, his body was opened to draw them out, and a huge daily quantity of lice and pestilent pus flowed out, with such a stench that no one could endure his presence. Witness John Bouchier, in an oration composed in praise of Philip.

units.la: LXIII. Non minus horrendum fatum mansit ante illud tempus aliquot Galliae reges, quorum permissu & jussu Evangelici ipsorum subditi diras persequutiones sunt passi. Heinricus II. frequentiac laetospectaculo concurrens cum Mongomerio comite, confractis utrinque hastis, aperta forte casside, in oculo ex trunci secundaria percussio ne tantum vulnus accepit, ut paucis diebus post, exhaustis acerrimis doloribus, obierit, anno MDLIX. mense Iulio: quum paulo ante mortem adadversam Bastiliam respiciens, & Senatorum, qui in ea capti detinebantur, recordatus dixisset, Vereri se[?], ne injuriam innocentibus hominibus fecisset. Carolus IX. Heinrici filius, in suomet sanguine, quem tantè ante copia profuderat, in Sanbartholomaeà praesertim lanienà, suffocatus periit: à quo toto tempore, quod supervixit, tam diris horroribus nocturnis infestabatur, ut somnum amplius capere nequiret. Heinricus III. ejus frater, à Iacobo Clemente Senensi, Monacho ordinis Praedicatorum, litteras ei offerente, cultro acuto oblongo in imo ventre vulneratus occubuit anno MDLXXXIX. quum anno proximè elapso in comitiis Blaesensibus Heinricum Principem Guisium ad d. XIII. Decembr. & postridie Ludoicum Cardinalem, Heinrici fratrem, saevum utrunque Ecclesiae Dei persequutorem, pugionibus & hastis confodi, eorumque cadavera calce vivâ, ad id ex consilio chirurgi paratâ, ne cineres superessent, consumi procurasset.
units.tr: LXIII. No less dreadful a fate befell, before that time, several kings of France, by whose permission and command their Evangelical subjects suffered terrible persecutions. Henry II, while jousting in the presence of a joyful crowd against Count Montgomery, with lances broken on both sides, had his visor by chance open, and received from a splinter of the lance a blow to the eye so severe that a few days later, worn out by most bitter pains, he died, in July 1559. Shortly before his death, looking towards the Bastille and remembering the senators who were held prisoner there, he had said that he feared he had done an injury to innocent men. Charles IX, son of Henry, perished suffocated in his own blood, which he had shed so copiously shortly before, especially in the slaughter of St Bartholomew; throughout the whole time he survived he was so harassed by terrible nocturnal horrors that he could no longer get any sleep. Henry III, his brother, was wounded in the lower belly by a long sharp knife offered him by Jacques Clément, a Dominican friar of Sens, who presented letters to him, and he died in 1589. In the previous year, at the Assembly of Blois, he had had Henry, Duke of Guise, stabbed with daggers and spears on 23 December, and the next day Louis, Cardinal and brother of Henry, both savage persecutors of the Church of God; and on the advice of a surgeon he had their corpses consumed with quicklime, prepared for this purpose, so that not even ashes should remain.

units.la: LXIIII. Haec, & alia exempla, quae sigillatim enumerare est ἐκτὸς τοῦ λόγου[?], satis ostendunt, verum esse illud Psalmi CIV. Deus non permittit cuiquam opprimere suos fideles: quin etiam reges propter illos reprehendit & castigat. Et quamvis multi saepe persequutores nihilo deterius habent in hoc seculo: tamen Deus poenas de eis sumit in futuro, ubi cruciatuum non est finis. De his enim ratum est illud Abrahami ad epulonem divitem: Bona tua recepisti in vita tua: nunc autem cruciaris, Luc. 16.25. Econtrario fideles etsi infinitis in hac terra calamitatibus à Tyrannis afficiuntur, vitâ denique ipsa corporali privantur: tamen privari non possunt cælesti & æterna, quod Dominus his claris verbis testatur, Corpus equidem trucidant: ast animā haud possunt trucidare, Matt.10.28.
units.tr: LXIV. These and other examples, which it would be beyond our purpose to list one by one, sufficiently show that that saying of Psalm 104 is true: God does not allow anyone to oppress his faithful; indeed he rebukes and chastises kings on their account. And although many persecutors often fare no worse in this age, yet God exacts punishment from them in the future life, where there is no end of torments. For concerning these, that saying of Abraham to the rich glutton is certain: "You received your good things in your life; but now you are tormented," Luke 16:25. On the contrary, the faithful, although they are afflicted by tyrants with infinite calamities in this earth, and are at last deprived of bodily life itself, yet cannot be deprived of the heavenly and eternal life, which the Lord attests in these clear words: "They indeed kill the body, but they cannot kill the soul," Matt. 10:28.

units.la: LXV. Et quomodo, obsecro, is, qui rationem habet non passercu-lorum tantum minutissimorum, sed etiam capitis nostri pilorum, rei tam parvæ, vilis, exilis, abjectæ & despectæ, quam revera pili quispi-am non faciat, sic, ut nullus eorum sine voluntate ejus, ex capite aut corpore nostro pereat aut amittatur, rationem non habeat Ecclesiæ, dilectissimæ sponsæ suæ: pro qua ipse met se exposuit, quam proprio suo met sanguine acquisivit, quam in suomet latibulo sedere, in suamet umbrâ pernoctare testatur? cujus se receptum, portionem, calicem su-turum promisit, ut à rabidis istis canibus, lupis, ursis, leonibus, leo-pardis, tigribus, aliisque belluis, quas tristes illi persequutores ad vi-rum referunt, allatretur ac dilanietur?
units.tr: LXV. And how, I beg you, can he who takes account not only of the tiniest sparrows but also of the hairs of our head, a thing so small, cheap, slight, abject and despised that no one would really value a single hair, so that not one of them perishes or is lost from our head or body without his will, fail to take account of his Church, his most beloved bride, for whom he exposed himself, whom he acquired with his own blood, and of whom he testifies that she sits in his own hiding-place and spends the night in his own shadow? To whose refuge and portion and cup he promised to give over, so that she might be barked at and torn by those rabid dogs, wolves, bears, lions, leopards, tigers, and other beasts, which those sad persecutors refer to a man?

units.la: LXVI. Homines fideles memores certæ ac gloriosæ victoriæ contra persequutiones, frequenter apud se reputet illa consolationis plenissima verba, Hi sunt, qui venerunt ex afflictione illâ magnâ, & laverunt stolas suas, ac dealbârunt eas in sanguine agni. Ideo sunt ante thronum Dei, & serviunt ei die ac nocte in templo ejus: & qui insidet throno, obumbrabit eos. Non esurient amplius, neque sitient amplius, nec in eos incidet sol, neque æstus: quoniam Agnus, qui in medio throni est, pascet eos, & deducet eos ad vivos fontes aquarum: & abstersurus est Deus omnem lacrymam ab oculis eorum, Apoc.7.
units.tr: LXVI. Let faithful men, mindful of the certain and glorious victory against persecutions, often ponder in themselves those words full of consolation: "These are they who came out of that great tribulation, and washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them. They shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more, nor shall the sun fall on them, nor any heat; for the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and lead them to living fountains of waters; and God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes," Rev. 7.

units.la: LXVII. Quod reliquum est, cæli terræq; e nihilo conditorem, supplices veneremur, ut, quum Christi Ecclesiam, hoc etiam ævo, vehementer concuti passim videamus, illam, contra tot vafra consilia & cruentas machinationes, inter tot in fidæ Bellonæ casus horribiliter fluctuantem, protegat, tueatur, conservet: nec permittat, ut exstincta verbi sui luce adversarii communes dicant, Ubi nunc est Deus istorum? ubi est Evangelium istorum? Etenim si unius hominis permotus precibus benignus Deus, pater miserationum, solis inhibuit cursum: quis obse-ro dubitet, quin tot fidelium ubique dispersorum communibus votis adductus, cursum malorum, quæ ipsos circumstipant, benignè sit inhi-biturus, ad gloriam nominis sui, & Ecclesiæ totius salutem?
units.tr: LXVII. As for the rest, let us humbly worship the Creator of heaven and earth out of nothing, so that, since we see the Church of Christ, even in this age, violently shaken on every side, he may protect, guard and preserve her, tossed horribly among so many crafty plots and bloody machinations, amid so many chances of faithless Bellona; and may not permit the adversaries, once the light of his word is extinguished, to say in common, "Where now is their God? where is their Gospel?" For if God, gracious and father of mercies, was moved by the prayers of one man and stopped the course of the sun, who, I beg you, can doubt that he, moved by the common prayers of so many faithful scattered everywhere, will graciously check the course of the evils that surround them, for the glory of his name and the salvation of the whole Church?

units.tr: FINIS

units.la: THEODORETUS.
units.tr: THEODORETUS.

units.la: Veluti quondam rubus ille, quem vidit Moses, ardore ignis non est absumtus: ita nec Christianos impiorum bellis petitos tela hostilia consumserunt: quin potius sicut lignato-ribus sylvam caedentibus multo plures pullulant propagi-nes a radicibus, quam sunt rami, qui inciduntur: ita nunc quo-que compluribus interfectis, multo plures quotidie ad do-ctrinam Evangelicam accedebant, cruorque ille caesorum corporum irrigatio quaedam erat novis emergentib.plantis.
units.tr: As the bramble that Moses saw was not consumed by the heat of the fire, so the Christians assailed by the wars of the impious were not destroyed by hostile weapons; rather, just as woodcutters felling a forest find that many more shoots spring up from the roots than the branches that are cut off, so now too, though many were slain, far more people each day came to the Evangelical doctrine, and that blood of the slaughtered bodies was a kind of watering for the newly sprouting plants.

units.la: TERTULLIANUS ad Persequutores.
units.tr: TERTULLIANUS ad Persequutores.

units.la: Cruciate, torquete, atterite. Probatio enim est innocentiae nostrae iniquitas vestra. Ideo nos haec pati Deus patitur. Exquisitior quaeque crudelitas vestra illecebra est magis sectae. Plures efficimur, quoties metimur a vobis: semen est sanguis Christianorum. Quum damnamur a vobis, absolvimur, &c. quod Poeta Christianus signanter his verbis expressit:
units.tr: Cut, torment, grind down. For your iniquity is the proof of our innocence. That is why God allows us to suffer these things. Every more refined cruelty of yours is a lure to the sect. We are made more numerous whenever we are mown down by you: the blood of Christians is seed. When we are condemned by you, we are acquitted, etc., which a Christian poet expressed pointedly in these words:

units.la: Sanguine fundata est Ecclesia: sanguine crevit: Sanguine succrevit: sanguine finis erit.
units.tr: The Church was founded in blood, grew in blood, rose up in blood: by blood it will come to an end.
